question: What types of works, undertakings, or businesses are considered 'federal work, undertaking or business' under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Federal Works, Undertakings, and Businesses Under the Canada Labour Code

### Definition of "Federal Work, Undertaking or Business"

Section 2 of the Canada Labour Code defines "federal work, undertaking or business" as encompassing a broad range of activities. The definition includes:

>
"(a) a work, undertaking or business operated or carried on for or in connection with navigation and shipping, whether inland or maritime, including the operation of ships and transportation by ship anywhere in Canada, (b) a railway, canal, telegraph or other work or undertaking connecting any province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province, (c) a line of ships connecting a province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province, (d) a ferry between any province and any other province or between any province and any country other than Canada, (e) aerodromes, aircraft or a line of air transportation, (f) a radio broadcasting station, (g) a bank or an authorized foreign bank within the meaning of section 2 of the Bank Act , (h) a work or undertaking that, although wholly situated within a province, is before or after its execution declared by Parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces, (i) a work, undertaking or business outside the exclusive legislative authority of the legislatures of the provinces, and (j) a work, undertaking or activity in respect of which federal laws within the meaning of section 2 of the Oceans Act apply pursuant to section 20 of that Act and any regulations made pursuant to paragraph 26(1)(k) of that Act..."

### Types of Activities Included

The definition specifies several categories of activities that fall under this classification. These include:

*   **Transportation:** This includes various forms of transportation, such as
"...navigation and shipping, whether inland or maritime, including the operation of ships and transportation by ship anywhere in Canada..."
"...railway, canal, telegraph or other work or undertaking connecting any province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province..." and
"...a line of ships connecting a province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province..."
*   **Aviation:** "Aerodromes, aircraft or a line of air transportation" are also considered federal works, undertakings, or businesses.
*   **Financial Institutions:
"...a bank or an authorized foreign bank within the meaning of section 2 of the Bank Act..." falls under this definition.
*   **Activities for the Benefit of Canada:
"...a work or undertaking that, although wholly situated within a province, is before or after its execution declared by Parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces..." is included.
*   **Activities Outside Provincial Jurisdiction:
"...a work, undertaking or business outside the exclusive legislative authority of the legislatures of the provinces..." is also covered.
*   **Oceans Act Activities:** Activities related to the Oceans Act are also included.

This comprehensive definition ensures that a wide array of federally regulated industries and businesses are subject to the Canada Labour Code.

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-7_27", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Report of the Expert Panel on Modern Federal Labour Standards", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Non-standard work and Part III of the  Code** Part III of the Code applies to, and in respect of, employees employed in or in  connection to any federal work, undertaking or business (including employees of  Crown corporations and excluding the federal public service). Part III is the  only labour standards legislation in Canada that does not include a definition  of "employee". Recent changes to Part III set a precedent for extending protections  to some workers (that is, beyond employees), both in terms of coverage and  effective access to such protections. Part III does not currently treat independent contractors as employees.  In the application of Part III, binary determinations of whether someone is a  true employee (who would be covered by Part III) or a true independent  contractor (who would not be covered by Part III) are therefore made on a  regular basis by workers and employers and, when complaints are brought  forward, on a case-by-case basis by Labour Program inspectors, adjudicators and  the courts.Footnote 38 Part I (Industrial Relations) of the Code does recognize the existence  of "dependent contractors" and treats them as employees. In particular, Part I  defines a "dependent contractor" as:  the owner, purchaser or lessee of a vehicle used  for hauling, other than on rails or tracks, livestock, liquids, goods,  merchandise or other materials, who is a party to a contract, oral or in  writing, under the terms of which they are:           required to provide the vehicle by means of  which they perform the contract and to operate the vehicle in accordance with  the contract; and entitled to retain for their own use from time  to time any sum of money that remains after the cost of their performance of  the contract is deducted from the amount they are paid, in accordance with the  contract, for that performance;    a fisher who,  pursuant to an arrangement to which the fisher is a party, is entitled to a  percentage or other part of the proceeds of a joint fishing venture in which  the fisher participates with other persons; and any other person who, whether or not employed  under a contract of employment, performs work or services for another person on  such terms and conditions that they are, in relation to that other person, in a  position of economic dependence on, and under an obligation to perform duties  for, that other person  The rationale for providing dependent contractors with rights under Part  I stems from arguments put forward by Harry Arthurs in the 1960s (Arthurs,  1967). Arthurs argued that dependent contractors should not be excluded from  collective bargaining simply because their employment relationship did not  resemble a traditional employer-employee relationship. A key point was that  collective bargaining is a means of correcting a power imbalance and, because  dependent contractors occupy the same labour market space as employees, they  should be eligible for unionization.  The Code also offers certain protections to both union and non-union  employees when a business or part of a business is sold, leased, merged or  otherwise transferred. Part I allows a bargaining agent to continue to  represent its unionized employees after such a sale or transfer, and allows the  collective agreement to remain in place until it expires. This is known as  "successorship rights".Footnote 39 The  new employer is bound by the existing collective agreement.  Part III provides that, when a federal work, undertaking or business, is  transferred from one employer to another, the employment of employees is deemed  to be continuous, notwithstanding the transfer. This is referred to as  "continuity of employment".Footnote 40 Continuity of employment is required to establish and retain entitlement to  protections and benefits under Part III that are only granted after completing  a period of continuous employment with the same employer (for example, unjust  dismissal, sick leave, bereavement and parental leaves and termination pay). Until recently, neither of these provisions applied when a contract was  retendered. This is commonly referred to as "contract flipping". Under the  amendments to section 189 made in the Budget Implementation Act, 2018, No. 2 (BIA 2), continuity of employment will now be  protected when a contract is retendered and the second employer becomes responsible  for carrying out any federal work, undertaking or business, or part of one. It  will also be protected when the work was previously regulated at the provincial  or territorial level.  BIA 2 also made other important amendments to Part III to:   Prohibit  employers from paying part-time, temporary, causal or seasonal employees a  lower wage than other employees simply because of their employment status if  they are doing substantially the same work under similar conditions, unless the  difference in rates of pay are based on objective factors (for example,  seniority, merit); Require  employers to provide all employees, regardless of their status, with  information about labour standards requirements, their conditions of employment  and promotional opportunities; and  Prohibit  temporary help agencies from charging a fee to an employee in connection with  assigning the employee to perform work for a client and paying an employee at a  lower rate than the rate paid by the client to its employees.  When  implemented, these changes are expected to reduce economic incentives for  employers to use non-standard forms of employment.  The recent changes will  also improve access to entitlements for those covered by Part III by:  eliminating the continuous employment requirements for general holiday pay,  sick leave, maternity and parental leave, leave related to critical illness and  leave related to death or disappearance of a child; and reducing the continuous  employment requirement for three weeks of paid vacation from 6 years to 5  years. This will assist temporary, seasonal and casual employees in becoming  eligible for statutory entitlements. The Expert Panel notes, however, that the  concept of "continuous employment" is not defined in the Code.  Other changes introduced through BIA 2 will  help prevent misclassification and protect misclassified employees.  Specifically, an employer will be prohibited from treating an  employee as if they are not their employee in order to avoid their obligations  under Part III or to deprive the employee of their rights under Part III.  Moreover, if in any proceeding in respect of a complaint made under Part III  the employer alleges that the complainant is not their employee, the burden of  proof is on the employer.  The Expert Panel believes it is important to observe that the intent element sets the initial burden of proof on the shoulders  of the employee, who must establish the employer’s intent to avoid obligations  or deprive the worker of their entitlements under the Code. Nevertheless, this  amendment is likely to send a signal to employers and workers about misclassification  and, in that sense, is proactive.  The BIA 2 changes received  Royal Assent in December 2018 and are coming into force as necessary  regulations are put in place.  Finally, Part III has recently been amended to provide greater  protection for individuals in the FRPS in another form of non-standard work,  namely unpaid internships.Footnote 41 This  was done through Bill C-63, the Budget Implementation Act,  2017, No. 1, which received Royal Assent in December  2017. Once in force, which is anticipated to be in 2020, the new provisions  will prohibit unpaid internships in the FRPS unless they are part of an  educational program and make sure, through regulations, that any unpaid interns  whose internships are part of such a program and who are unpaid receive labour  standards protections appropriate to this type of non-standard work. The  changes will come into force as soon as necessary regulations are in place.  Taken together, these changes introduced as  part of the federal government’s modernizing federal labour standards agenda  make important strides to better address non-standard work. However, there is  still more to be done."

question: What types of workers are considered employees under the Canada Labour Code, and what are some of the key terms and phrases defined in the Code that relate to labour relations?
answer:
## Types of Workers Considered Employees Under the Canada Labour Code

### Definition of "Employee" and Related Concepts

The Canada Labour Code, specifically Part III, applies to "employees" working in federally regulated businesses. However, the Code also recognizes and provides certain protections for other types of workers.

The document states:
"Part I (Industrial Relations) of the Code does recognize the existence  of "dependent contractors" and treats them as employees." This indicates that dependent contractors are considered employees under the Code, despite their employment relationship not fitting the traditional employer-employee model.

### Definition of "Dependent Contractor"

The Code defines a "dependent contractor" as:

>
"...the owner, purchaser or lessee of a vehicle used  for hauling, other than on rails or tracks, livestock, liquids, goods,  merchandise or other materials, who is a party to a contract, oral or in  writing, under the terms of which they are:           required to provide the vehicle by means of  which they perform the contract and to operate the vehicle in accordance with  the contract; and entitled to retain for their own use from time  to time any sum of money that remains after the cost of their performance of  the contract is deducted from the amount they are paid, in accordance with the  contract, for that performance;    a fisher who,  pursuant to an arrangement to which the fisher is a party, is entitled to a  percentage or other part of the proceeds of a joint fishing venture in which  the fisher participates with other persons; and any other person who, whether or not employed  under a contract of employment, performs work or services for another person on  such terms and conditions that they are, in relation to that other person, in a  position of economic dependence on, and under an obligation to perform duties  for, that other person..."

This definition highlights that a dependent contractor is considered an employee when they are economically dependent on another person and obligated to perform duties for them, even if not formally employed.

### Other Worker Categories and Protections

The Code also offers protections to both unionized and non-unionized employees in situations like business transfers, as noted in the document:
"Part I allows a bargaining agent to continue to  represent its unionized employees after such a sale or transfer, and allows the  collective agreement to remain in place until it expires." This ensures continuity of employment and rights for workers during business transitions.

Furthermore, the Code addresses non-standard forms of employment, such as unpaid internships, aiming to prevent exploitation and ensure fair labour standards. The document mentions:
"Part III has recently been amended to provide greater  protection for individuals in the FRPS in another form of non-standard work,  namely..."

## Key Terms and Phrases Defined in the Code

### Continuity of Employment

The concept of "continuity of employment" is crucial for establishing and retaining entitlement to certain benefits under Part III. The document explains:
"Continuity of employment is required to establish and retain entitlement to  protections and benefits under Part III that are only granted after completing  a period of continuous employment with the same employer (for example, unjust  dismissal, sick leave, bereavement and parental leaves and termination pay)."

### Successorship Rights

"Successorship rights" are designed to protect the rights of employees when a business is sold, leased, merged, or transferred. The document states:
"Part I allows a bargaining agent to continue to  represent its unionized employees after such a sale or transfer, and allows the  collective agreement to remain in place until it expires. This is known as  "successorship..."

### Misclassification

The Code includes provisions to prevent employers from misclassifying employees as independent contractors to avoid their obligations. The document notes:
"Moreover, if in any proceeding in respect of a complaint made under Part III  the employer alleges that the complainant is not their employee, the burden of  proof is on the employer." This shift in burden of proof aims to deter misclassification practices.

### Intent

The document mentions that the initial burden of proof in cases of misclassification lies with the employee to demonstrate the employer's intent to avoid obligations or deprive the worker of their rights. This highlights the importance of proving the employer's intention in such cases.

question: Who does this part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations) apply to?
answer:
## Application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code

This section outlines the scope of application for Part I of the Canada Labour Code, specifically focusing on who is covered by its provisions. The application extends to various entities and individuals involved in federal work, undertakings, and businesses.

### General Application to Employees and Employers

Section 4 states:
"Section 4 This Part applies in respect of employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business, in respect of the employers of all such employees in their relations with those employees and in respect of trade unions and employers’ organizations composed of those employees or..."

This indicates that Part I applies to
"...employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business..."  Furthermore, it extends to the relationship between employers and employees, as well as to trade unions and employer organizations composed of these employees or employers. This broad application ensures that the provisions of Part I impact all stakeholders within the federal employment landscape.

### Specific Applications and Exceptions

Several sections detail specific applications and exceptions to the general rule.

#### Application to Federal Public Administration

Section 123 specifies that
"This Part applies to the federal public administration and to persons employed in the federal public administration to the extent provided for under Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act..." This clarifies that the federal public administration is subject to Part I, with certain provisions being governed by Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act.

#### Application to Crown Corporations

Section 121.1 states:
"Section 121.1 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section indicates that Part I can be applied to employees of Crown corporations, provided that the Governor in Council issues a regulation directing its application. This highlights a degree of flexibility in extending the Code's provisions to Crown corporations.

#### Application to Provincial Crown Corporations

Section 121.1 also includes a "Marginal note: Exclusion from application," which suggests that there may be specific circumstances under which Part I does *not* apply to employees of provincial Crown corporations. However, the exact details of this exclusion are not provided within the excerpt.

### Overall Scope

In summary, Part I of the Canada Labour Code applies broadly to employees working in federal work, undertakings, and businesses, as well as to the relationships between employers and employees, and to trade unions and employer organizations.  It also extends to the federal public administration and, subject to regulation, to Crown corporations. The inclusion of specific sections like 121.1 demonstrates that the application of Part I is not uniform and can be tailored to specific entities within the federal employment sector.

question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council exclude a corporation from the operation of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations)?
answer:
## Exclusion of Corporations from the Canada Labour Code (Part I)

### General Authority for Exclusion

The Governor in Council has the authority to exclude corporations from the application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code through regulation. This power is outlined in several sections, particularly CLC-266, CLC-158, CLC-265, and CLC-121.1.

CLC-266 states:
"Section 266 (1) The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section establishes the broad power to exclude
"...any employment, or any class or classes of employment..." associated with specific works or undertakings regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Exclusion of Provincial Crown Corporations

CLC-158 and CLC-265 specifically address the exclusion of provincial Crown corporations. Both sections state:
"Section 158 The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."
"Section 265 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

These sections indicate that the Governor in Council can direct the application of Part I to or exclude it from employment within provincial Crown corporations that act as agents of the Crown and whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Additional Conditions for Exclusion

CLC-5 provides further details on the conditions under which the Governor in Council can exclude corporations. It states:
"Section 5 (1) This Part applies in respect of any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada and in respect of the employees of any such corporation, except any such corporation, and the employees thereof, that the Governor in Council excludes from the operation of this Part."

This section indicates that the Governor in Council can exclude corporations from the operation of Part I, but only those corporations for which a minister of the Crown, the Treasury Board, or the Governor in Council is authorized to establish or approve terms and conditions of employment.

In summary, the Governor in Council can exclude corporations from the application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code, particularly provincial Crown corporations, through regulation. This exclusion is often linked to corporations operating under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act and is subject to conditions related to the authorization of employment terms.

question: Who bears the burden of proof in determining whether a person is an employee of an employer in proceedings under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Burden of Proof in Employment Status Determinations under the Canada Labour Code

### General Presumption of Employment

Several sections of the Canada Labour Code establish a presumption that a person who is paid remuneration by an employer is an employee.
"Section 123.1 For greater certainty, nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to abrogate or derogate from the rights provided for under the Canadian Human Rights Act..." This section, while not directly addressing the burden of proof, underscores the importance of the presumption of employment established elsewhere in the Code.
"Section 167.01 (1) A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer." This is a core provision, clearly stating the initial presumption.
"Section 6.1 (1) A person — other than a person who performs management functions or is employed in a confidential capacity in matters relating to industrial relations — who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer." This section reinforces the presumption, with a slight variation in the scope of individuals covered.

### Who Must Prove the Contrary?

The burden of overcoming this presumption lies with the employer.
"Section 123.1 For greater certainty, nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to abrogate or derogate from the rights provided for under the Canadian Human Rights Act..." This section, while not directly addressing the burden of proof, underscores the importance of the presumption of employment established elsewhere in the Code.
"Section 123.3 If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer." This section explicitly states that if an employer claims someone is *not* an employee, they must provide evidence to support that claim.
"Section 167.2 If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer." This section reiterates the same principle, reinforcing that the employer bears the responsibility of proving that a worker is not an employee.

### Exception to the Burden of Proof

It is important to note an exception to this rule.
"Section 123.1 For greater certainty, nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to abrogate or derogate from the rights provided for under the Canadian Human Rights Act..." This section, while not directly addressing the burden of proof, underscores the importance of the presumption of employment established elsewhere in the Code.
"Section 167.1 An employer is prohibited from treating an employee as if they were not their employee." This section highlights that an employer cannot unilaterally decide someone is not an employee without justification.

In summary, under the Canada Labour Code, the burden of proof rests on the employer to demonstrate that a person is *not* an employee when the initial presumption of employment exists. This presumption is a significant factor in determining employment status in various proceedings under the Code.

question: How can the Minister and the Board assist in collective bargaining for certain projects under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Assistance in Collective Bargaining for Major Projects

### Major Projects and Expedited Process

The Canada Labour Code outlines provisions for facilitating collective bargaining on a project basis, particularly for what the Minister determines to be "major projects."
"Section 7 Nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to prevent the establishment of agreements on a project basis and where all the parties in a collective bargaining relationship identify themselves to the Minister as being engaged in a project that the Minister determines to be a major project, the Minister and the Board shall act as expeditiously as possible to facilitate the collective bargaining process involving those parties."

This section explicitly states that if parties identify themselves to the Minister as being involved in a major project, the Minister and the Board are obligated to act "as expeditiously as possible" to facilitate the collective bargaining process. This indicates a proactive role for both the Minister and the Board in ensuring a swift and efficient bargaining process for these projects.

### Minister's Role in Directing the Board

The Minister also has the authority to directly intervene in collective bargaining disputes.
"Section 80 (1) Where an employer or a bargaining agent is required, by notice given under section 48, to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the first collective agreement between the parties with respect to the bargaining unit for which the bargaining agent has been certified and the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have otherwise been met, the Minister may, if the Minister considers it necessary or advisable, at any time thereafter direct the Board to inquire into the dispute and, if the Board considers it advisable, to settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement between the parties."

This passage highlights the Minister's power to direct the Board to investigate and potentially settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement. This intervention can be crucial in resolving disputes and ensuring a fair outcome for all parties involved in a major project. The Minister's decision to direct the Board is based on whether it is "necessary or advisable," demonstrating a flexible approach to facilitating the bargaining process.

LABOUR-REPORTS-7_61:

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-7_61", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Report of the Expert Panel on Modern Federal Labour Standards", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Anti-reprisal protection for  concerted activity** Studies  show that many workers are unlikely to speak out about problems in the  workplace if they do not have access to collective voice mechanisms because  they fear reprisal. This is particularly true for non-unionized workers and  those in non-standard work, as well as women. For instance, using survey  data collected in 2005, Lewchuk (2013) concludes that "the precariously  employed were six to seven times more likely to report that raising health and  safety issues would have negative employment consequences".  In the United States, section 7 of the National Labor  Relations Act (NLRA) provides non-supervisory employees, both union and  non-union, with the right to engage in "concerted activity for the purpose of  collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection". As defined by the  U.S. Supreme Court, "mutual aid and protection" includes employees’ efforts to  "improve current terms and conditions of employment or otherwise improve their  lots as employees through channels outside the immediate employee/employer  relationship"Footnote 135 The Act does not limit the manner, time or place in which  employees engage in "concerted activity". While section 7 lists workers’ protected rights, section 8 makes it  unlawful for an employer to "interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in  the exercise of the rights guaranteed in section 7". The employer’s conduct will be considered as retaliation if  it tends to interfere with the free exercise of employee rights under the NLRA  and "demonstrating motive or actual coercion is therefore not generally  required" (Rogers & Archer, 2016). Sections 7 and 8 were introduced  when the NLRA was enacted in 1935.  Section 7 of the NLRA protects concerted activities by  unionized workers and non-unionized workers, whether they are seeking to  unionize or not (Rogers & Archer, 2016). The spectrum of protected  concerted activities is wide and includes concerted complaints or grievances  presented to employers regarding compensation, benefits or working conditions,  as well as informal discussions between employees about their working  conditions (Fullerton & Millman, 2008). The protected activities must generally be undertaken by two or more  employees seeking to improve their terms or conditions of employment.  Thus, two or more employees addressing their employer about  improving their pay will be exercising their right to protected concerted  activity. However, the  protection can also extend to the actions of one employee, on the condition  that such actions have "the object of initiating or inducing or preparing  for group action or [have] some relation to group action in the interest of the  employees." Footnote 136 Footnote 137 Section 7 will apply when an  employee speaks to his employer on behalf of one or more co-workers about  improving workplace conditions (NLRB, n.d.). Non-union work stoppages and  walkouts are generally protected,Footnote 138 unless they are "unlawful, violent, […] in breach of contract [or]  "irresponsible" because they threaten property damage" (Rogers & Archer,  2016). Section 7 has been interpreted to  extend the "Weingarten" rule (that is, that an employee in a  unionized workplace may request the presence of a union representative at an  investigatory interview which employee reasonably believes might result in  disciplinary action) to cover employees in non-union workplaces.Footnote 139 The use of social media is, to a  certain extent, protected by section 7 as employees have the right to address  work-related issues and share information about pay, benefits, and working  conditions with coworkers on Facebook, YouTube, and other social media. To be  protected, the use of social media must have some relation to group action, or  seek to initiate, induce or prepare for group action, or bring a group  complaint to the attention of management (Neylon O’Brien, 2011; Bemberg, 2018).  For  instance, an employer's decision to  dismiss an employee who posted a comment on Facebook encouraging a terminated  colleague to hire a lawyer and sue the company was over-ruled by the National  Labor Relations Board (NLRB). The Facebook comment was found to be a protected concerted activity  that did not interfere with the employer’s operations.Footnote 140 However, complaints that are made  publicly and are maliciously false will not be protected.Footnote 141 Many employers have social media policies that aim to limit what their  employee may publish. When such policies are found to be overly broad (that is,  when they prohibit lawful activities either explicitly or by being too vague),  the NLRB can order the employer to rescind or modify them.Footnote 142 Protected  concerted activities provide statutory protection against reprisals for  employees wishing to collectively voice concerns. This form of collective voice  is independent from the employer who is required to not interfere. The American  experience suggests that it can be useful in circumstances in which employees  face particularly egregious working conditions and are otherwise unable to  bring about change or improvements.  For  example, in a leading 1962 case (NLRB v. Washington  Aluminum) workers had  complained about the cold temperatures in the facility during the winter. Footnote 143 On a particularly cold day workers arrived to  find the plant completely unheated and seven walked out. The U.S. Supreme Court  upheld the NLRB’s ruling that the company’s termination of these workers was  unlawful. Similarly, in a more recent case a group of restaurant workers who  had been terminated after protesting working conditions appealed to the NLRB  which ordered them reinstated (Greenhouse, 2015). A search on Lexis Advance US conducted in March  2019 yielded 8,993 NLRB cases dealing with section 7, going back as far as  1935. Although this is a small number over a period of more than 80 years, the  number of cases per year has grown substantially in recent years during a time  when private sector unionization has also fallen sharply. Figure 18  plots  the number of cases per year over the 1935 to 2019 period. The number has  increased significantly over the past two decades.   Figure 18: Number of cases before the NLRB  (section 7 NLRA), 1935–2019   Figure 18 - Text version    Dates Number of cases   1935–1939 396   1940–1944 487   1945–1949 24   1950–1954 42   1955–1959 45   1960–1964 102   1965–1969 187   1970–1974 430   1975-1979 916   1980–1984 854   1985–1989 445   1990–1994 443   1995–1999 329   2000–2004 335   2005-2009 753   2010–2014 1806   2015–2019 1565      Source:  Panel analysis of NLRB/Lexis Advance US.    However, it is important to note that the number of cases  related to section 7 is likely to understate the importance of this provision  because of the "threat effect"—employers who are aware of the law and previous  interpretations by the courts will adjust their behaviour in order to be in  compliance and avoid a costly lawsuit.  Unlike some other  mechanisms, the NLRA protection for concerted activity has the advantage of  having been available and used in the United States, a country that shares many  commonalities with Canada’s labour relations system. It is unclear whether the  collective voice achievable with the support of such a protection might develop  into more sustained collective activity, such as achieving union  representation. Nevertheless, adopting a protection for concerted activity  might be helpful for workers in the FRPS with particularly poor working  conditions.  Recommendation 25: The Panel recommends introducing  a protection for concerted activities in Part III of the Code.  Our recommendation regarding  this protection is two-fold. First, Part III should state that employees have a  right to participate in concerted activities. Second, employees  who have been dismissed,  suspended, laid-off, demoted or otherwise disciplined because they have  exercised their right to concerted activity should be protected against such  reprisals.Footnote 144 Adding a protection for  concerted activity to Part III would also likely enhance workers’  willingness to join participatory initiatives channelled through community  organizations. The Panel views this right as a potentially useful incremental  change to Canada’s labour relations system in the FRPS and one that would bring  the Code more in line with recent Supreme Court interpretations of the  guarantee of freedom of association in section 2(d) of the Canadian Charter of  Rights and Freedoms."

question: What freedoms do employees and employers have regarding joining and participating in trade unions and employers' organizations?
answer:
## Employee and Employer Freedoms Regarding Trade Unions and Employers' Organizations

### Section 8 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 8 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the freedoms of both employees and employers concerning trade unions and employers' organizations.

#### Employee Freedom to Join and Participate
"Every employee is free to join the trade union of their choice and to participate in its lawful activities."

This section guarantees employees the fundamental right to self-determination in choosing a trade union and actively engaging in union activities. This freedom is crucial for collective bargaining, grievance procedures, and the overall promotion of workers' rights.

#### Employer Freedom to Join and Participate
"Every employer is free to join the employers’ organization of their choice and to participate in its lawful activities."

This provision ensures that employers also have the right to form and participate in organizations that represent their interests. Employers' organizations facilitate collective bargaining on behalf of employers, provide legal support, and promote consistent labor practices within industries.

### Additional Context from Other Documents

While Section 8 of the Canada Labour Code provides the foundational freedoms, other documents highlight related aspects of employee and employer rights.

#### Collective Voice for Non-Unionized Workers

The "Collective voice for non-unionized workers: Issue paper" discusses initiatives like Unifor's Community Chapters, which aim to provide non-unionized workers with avenues for collective voice and power. This demonstrates a broader recognition of the importance of collective action beyond traditional union structures.

#### Concerted Activity Rights

The
"Report of the Expert Panel on Modern Federal Labour Standards" (no source found for the quotation) details the concept of "anti-reprisal protection for concerted activity." This protection allows employees to engage in activities aimed at improving their working conditions without fear of retaliation. The document states,
"Studies  show that many workers are unlikely to speak out about problems in the  workplace if they do not have access to collective voice mechanisms because  they fear reprisal." This underscores the importance of freedom of expression and collective action for all employees, regardless of union affiliation.

#### Employer Restrictions on Interference

The "Unfair Practices: Employer interference in trade union" section of the Canada Labour Code (Section 94) outlines specific prohibitions against employers interfering with the formation or administration of trade unions and the representation of employees by a trade union. This reinforces the freedom of employees to organize and collectively bargain without employer interference.

question: What is the structure and composition of the Canada Industrial Relations Board according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Structure and Composition of the Canada Industrial Relations Board

### Section 9: Establishment of Board

Section 9 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the structure and composition of the Canada Industrial Relations Board.

#### Core Members
"(a) a Chairperson, to hold office on a full-time basis; (b) two or more Vice-Chairpersons, to hold office on a full-time basis, and any other Vice-Chairpersons, to hold office on a part-time basis, that the Governor in Council considers necessary to discharge the responsibilities of the Board; (c) not more than six other members, of which not more than three represent employees, and of which not more than three represent employers, to hold office on a full-time basis..."

This indicates that the Board is headed by a full-time Chairperson. It also includes one or more Vice-Chairpersons, who can serve on a full-time or part-time basis, depending on the needs of the Board.  Furthermore, the Board can have up to six additional full-time members, with a specific limit on the representation of employees and employers (maximum of three each).

#### Additional Members
"(d) any other part-time members, representing, in equal numbers, employees and employers, that the Governor in Council considers necessary to discharge the responsibilities of the Board; and (e) any other full-time or part-time members that the Governor in Council considers necessary to assist the Board in carrying out its functions under Parts II, III and IV."

The Board can also include part-time members representing both employees and employers, ensuring balanced representation.  Additionally, the Governor in Council can appoint other full-time or part-time members as needed to support the Board's functions under Parts II, III, and IV of the Act. This allows for flexibility in staffing the Board based on its workload and specific needs.

question: Who appoints the members of the Board, and what are the general requirements for their appointment and terms?
answer:
## Appointment of Board Members

### Appointment Authority

The Governor in Council appoints the members of the Board. This appointment is made on the recommendation of the Minister.
"The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons of the Board are to be appointed by the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister..."

### General Requirements for Appointment

Several requirements apply to the appointment of Board members:

*   **Citizenship/Residency:
"The members of the Board must be Canadian citizens or permanent residents within the meaning of subsection 2(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act..."
*   **Experience and Expertise:
"The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons must have experience and expertise in industrial relations."
*   **Consultation with Organizations:
"Subject to subsection (3), the members of the Board other than the Chairperson and the Vice-Chairpersons are to be appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation by the Minister with the organizations representative of employees or employers that the Minister considers appropriate..."

### Terms of Office

The terms of office for Board members vary depending on their position:

*   **Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons:
"...to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding five years each..."
*   **Other Members:
"...to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding three years each..."
*   **Members appointed pursuant to paragraph 9(2)(e):
"...to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding three years each..."

The terms are subject to removal by the Governor in Council at any time for cause.

question: What are the restrictions on members of the Board in terms of holding other employment or office?
answer:
## Restrictions on Board Members' Employment

### Full-Time Members

Section 11(1) of the Canada Labour Code states:
"The full-time members of the Board must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration." This indicates a strict restriction on full-time board members. They are prohibited from having any other paid position that could potentially create a conflict of interest or detract from their duties on the Board.

### Part-Time Members and Members Appointed Under Paragraph 9(2)(e)

Section 11(2) outlines the restrictions for part-time Vice-Chairpersons and members appointed pursuant to paragraph 9(2)(e). It specifies:
"A part-time Vice-Chairperson, or a member appointed pursuant to paragraph 9(2)(e), must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration and that is inconsistent with their duties under this Act." This means that while part-time members can hold other positions, those positions cannot conflict with their responsibilities on the Board. The key here is "inconsistent with their duties under this Act," suggesting a judgment will be made on a case-by-case basis regarding potential conflicts.

question: What happens to a member of the Board when their term of office expires or when they cease to be a member, and how does the Board ensure continuity in its operations?
answer:
## Reappointment and Continuity of Board Operations

### Reappointment of Board Members

Section 12(1) of the Canada Labour Code addresses the eligibility for reappointment.
"Section 12 (1) A member of the Board is eligible for reappointment on the expiration of any term of office in the same or another capacity."

This indicates that board members can be reappointed, allowing for continuity of experience and knowledge within the Board. This ensures that the Board can maintain its expertise and avoid disruption due to the departure of experienced members.

### Duties After Ceasing to be a Member

Section 12(2) outlines the circumstances under which a former board member can continue to perform duties.
"Where a member of the Board ceases to be a member of the Board for any reason other than removal, the member may, despite anything in this Part, at the request of the Chairperson, carry out and complete any duties or responsibilities that the member would otherwise have had if the member had not ceased to be a member, in connection with any matter that came before the Board while the member was still a member of the Board and in respect of which there was any proceeding in which the member participated as a member."

This provision allows for continuity by enabling a former member to complete ongoing tasks related to matters they were actively involved in while serving on the Board. This prevents unfinished business from being abandoned and ensures a smooth transition. The requirement for the Chairperson's request ensures that such arrangements are made only when necessary and with the appropriate authorization.

### Acting Chairperson

Section 12.03 addresses the situation when the Chairperson is absent or unable to act.
"Section 12.03 If the Chairperson of the Board is absent or unable to act or the office of Chairperson is vacant, a Vice-Chairperson designated by the Minister acts as Chairperson for the time being, and a Vice-Chairperson so designated has and may exercise all the powers and perform all the duties and functions of the Chairperson."

This ensures that the Board's operations are not disrupted by the absence of the Chairperson. A designated Vice-Chairperson can step in and fulfill the Chairperson's responsibilities, maintaining the Board's ability to function effectively.

### External Adjudicator

Section 12.001 introduces the possibility of using external adjudicators to ensure continuity in specific situations.
"(1) The Chairperson may, if the Chairperson considers it advisable, appoint an external adjudicator to determine any matter that comes before the Board under section 87.4 or Part II, III or IV."
"(2) An external adjudicator has all the powers, duties and functions that are conferred on the Board by this Act with respect to any matter for which they have been appointed."

This allows the Board to continue its work even when internal resources are unavailable or when specialized expertise is required. The external adjudicator assumes all the powers and duties of the Board in the specific matter, ensuring that the process continues without interruption.

question: What are the responsibilities of the Chairperson in terms of managing the work of the Board?
answer:
## Responsibilities of the Chairperson in Managing Board Work

### Section 12.01: Functions of Chairperson

Section 12.01 outlines the Chairperson's comprehensive supervisory and directorial responsibilities over the Board's work. These responsibilities are detailed in subsection (1) and include:

*   **Assignment of Matters to Panels:
"...the assignment and reassignment of matters that the Board is seized of to panels..."
    This indicates the Chairperson is responsible for distributing cases and issues to the appropriate panels for review and consideration. This ensures efficient handling of the Board's workload.

*   **Panel Composition and Vice-Chairperson Assignment:
"...the composition of panels and the assignment of Vice-Chairpersons to preside over panels..."
    The Chairperson plays a key role in determining the makeup of the panels and assigning Vice-Chairpersons to lead these panels. This suggests the Chairperson is involved in ensuring fair and effective panel operations.

*   **Scheduling Hearings:
"...the determination of the date, time and place of hearings..."
    The Chairperson is responsible for setting the schedule for hearings, which is a crucial aspect of managing the Board's workflow and ensuring timely proceedings.

*   **Conduct of Board Work:** "the conduct of the work of the Board"
    This is a broad responsibility indicating the Chairperson oversees the overall operations and processes of the Board.

*   **Management of Internal Affairs:** "the management of the Board’s internal affairs"
    The Chairperson is responsible for the administrative and organizational aspects of the Board, ensuring its smooth functioning.

### Section 12.02: Chairperson's Role in Meetings

While Section 12.02 primarily focuses on meetings, it indirectly relates to the Chairperson's management responsibilities. Section 12.02(1) states:
"The Chairperson convenes and presides over any meeting of the Board concerning the making of regulations under section 15." This highlights the Chairperson's role in initiating and leading discussions related to regulatory matters, which is a significant aspect of the Board's work.

### Section 12.03: Acting Chairperson

Section 12.03 outlines the process for an Acting Chairperson when the regular Chairperson is unavailable. This further emphasizes the importance of the Chairperson's role in ensuring the Board's continuous operation and effective management of its work.
"If the Chairperson of the Board is absent or unable to act or the office of Chairperson is vacant, a Vice-Chairperson designated by the Minister acts as Chairperson for the time being, and a Vice-Chairperson so designated has and may exercise all the powers and perform all the duties and functions of the Chairperson." This ensures that the Board's functions are not disrupted due to the Chairperson's absence.

question: What are the requirements for a quorum at a meeting of the Board for making regulations, and how may the composition of the quorum vary?
answer:
## Quorum Requirements for Board Meetings for Making Regulations

### General Quorum Requirements

Section 12.02(2) outlines the general requirements for a quorum when the Board is meeting to make regulations. It states:
"For the purposes of subsection (1), the following persons constitute a quorum: (a) subject to paragraph (b), the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and two other members representing, respectively, employees and employers; or (b) at a meeting held for the making of regulations respecting matters that are not governed by Part I, the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and, if two or more full-time members have been appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e), two of those members."

This indicates that a quorum generally requires the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons, and two members representing employees and employers. However, this composition can vary depending on the subject matter of the regulations being considered.

### Variation in Quorum Composition

The composition of the quorum can vary based on whether the regulations relate to matters governed by Part I of the Canada Labour Code.

*   **Regulations Governed by Part I:
"If, at a meeting referred to in subsection (1) held for the making of regulations respecting matters that are governed by Part I, there is an unequal number of members representing employers and employees, the Chairperson shall designate an equal number of members who are authorized to vote on the making of those regulations and who represent employers and employees respectively." This means that if there's an imbalance in representation between employee and employer members when dealing with matters under Part I, the Chairperson has the authority to designate an equal number of members from each group to ensure fair representation for voting purposes.

*   **Regulations Not Governed by Part I:
"...at a meeting held for the making of regulations respecting matters that are not governed by Part I, the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and, if two or more full-time members have been appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e), two of those members." In this case, the quorum consists of the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons, and two full-time members appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e), if applicable.

### Additional Considerations

Section 12.02(3) further clarifies that members representing employees or employers are not permitted to vote on regulations that are not governed by Part I. This ensures that the voting process is conducted by members who are not directly invested in the outcome of the regulations.

Section 12.03 addresses the situation where the Chairperson is absent or unable to act, stating that a Vice-Chairperson designated by the Minister acts as Chairperson for the time being. This ensures that meetings can continue even in the absence of the Chairperson.

question: What financial provisions are made for members of the Board in relation to their service, and what protection do they have from personal liability?
answer:
## Financial Provisions for Board Members

### Remuneration and Expenses

Section 12.04(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the financial provisions for Board members. It states:
"The full-time members of the Board shall be paid any remuneration, and the part-time members of the Board and members of the Board carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2) shall be paid any fees, that may be fixed by the Governor in Council."

This indicates that Board members, both full-time and part-time, are entitled to either remuneration or fees, the specific amount of which is determined by the Governor in Council. This ensures that Board members are compensated for their time and effort in fulfilling their duties.

Furthermore, Section 12.04(2) addresses travel and living expenses:
"The members of the Board are entitled to be paid reasonable travel and living expenses incurred by them in the course of their duties under this Act while absent from, in the case of full-time members, their ordinary place of work and, in the case of part-time members and members carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2), their ordinary place of residence."

This provision ensures that Board members are reimbursed for reasonable expenses incurred while performing their duties, including travel and accommodation.

## Protection from Personal Liability

### Limitation of Liability

Section 12.051 of the Canada Labour Code provides protection from personal liability for Board members:
"The Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members and external adjudicators are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act."

This section explicitly states that Board members are not personally liable for actions taken in good faith while performing their duties. This protection shields them from potential legal or criminal repercussions arising from their decisions or actions as Board members, as long as those actions were taken with a reasonable belief that they were in the best interest of the Board and its responsibilities. This provision encourages individuals to serve on the Board without fear of undue personal risk.

question: What actions can the Minister take upon receiving a request under Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Minister's Actions Upon Receiving a Request Under Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code

### Initial Measures

Upon receiving a request, the Minister has several options, as outlined in Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code:

**1. Information Gathering:
"...obtain, in an informal and expeditious manner, any information that the Minister considers necessary..."
This indicates the Minister can initiate the process by gathering information related to the request. The process is described as "informal and expeditious," suggesting a relatively quick and flexible approach to initial information gathering.

**2. Mediation Referral:
"...refer the matter for mediation, where the Minister is satisfied that the issues in relation to the request may be appropriately resolved by mediation..."
The Minister can suggest mediation as a means of resolving the issue. This option is contingent on the Minister's assessment that mediation is a suitable approach.

**3. Inquiry Referral to Governor in Council:
"...request the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08..."
The Minister can formally request the Governor in Council to initiate a more formal inquiry under Section 12.08 of the Canada Labour Code. This suggests that the Minister can escalate the matter to a higher level of investigation if deemed necessary.

**4. Advisory to Chairperson:
"...advise the Chairperson that the Minister considers that it is not necessary to take further measures under this section."
The Minister has the option to determine that no further action is required and inform the Chairperson accordingly. This indicates that the Minister has discretion in deciding whether to pursue the request further.



### Inquiry Process (as per Section 12.08)

The text also mentions the process that can be initiated by the Governor in Council upon the Minister's request:

**1. Appointment of a Judge:
"On receipt of a request referred to in paragraph 12.07(c), the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry."
If the Governor in Council agrees to proceed with an inquiry, they can appoint a judge of a superior court to lead the investigation.

**2. Judge's Powers:
"The judge has all the powers, rights and privileges that are vested in a superior court, including the power (a) to issue a summons requiring any person to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons to testify about all matters within that person’s knowledge relative to the inquiry and to produce any document or thing relative to the inquiry; and (b) to administer oaths and examine any person on oath."
The appointed judge is granted extensive powers, including the ability to compel testimony and access to documents.

**3. Staffing and Expertise:
"The judge may engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the judge in conducting the inquiry, establish the terms and conditions of their engagement and, with the approval of the Treasury Board, fix and pay their remuneration and expenses."
The judge can also hire experts to assist with the inquiry, ensuring a thorough and informed investigation.

question: What are the general principles guiding the conduct of an inquiry under the Canada Labour Code, particularly with respect to transparency, confidentiality, and the rights of parties involved?
answer:
## General Principles Guiding Inquiries Under the Canada Labour Code

### Transparency

The Canada Labour Code emphasizes transparency in the conduct of inquiries. Section 12.11(1) states,
"Subject to subsections (2) and (3), an inquiry must be conducted in public." This indicates a strong default principle of openness. The rationale behind this is to ensure accountability and allow for public scrutiny of the proceedings.

### Confidentiality

While inquiries are generally public, the Code recognizes situations where confidentiality is necessary. Section 12.11(2) allows the judge to take measures to ensure confidentiality if there is a
"...real and substantial risk that matters involving public security will be disclosed; (b) there is a real and substantial risk to the fairness of the inquiry such that the need to prevent disclosure outweighs the societal interest that the inquiry be conducted in public; or (c) there is a serious possibility that the life, liberty or security of a person will be endangered." This demonstrates a balancing approach, prioritizing public access while safeguarding sensitive information and ensuring a fair process.

Section 12.11(3) further addresses confidentiality in hearings related to applications under subsection (2), allowing the judge to take necessary measures to ensure confidentiality in those specific cases.

### Rights of Parties Involved

The Code explicitly outlines the rights of the individual subject to the inquiry. Section 12.13 states,
"The member who is the subject of the inquiry must be given reasonable notice of the subject-matter of the inquiry and of the time and place of any hearing and must be given an opportunity, in person or by counsel, to be heard at the hearing, to cross-examine witnesses and to present evidence." This ensures due process and allows the individual to defend themselves against the allegations.

Furthermore, Section 12.12(2) grants
"An interested party may, with leave of the judge, intervene in an inquiry on the terms and conditions that the judge considers appropriate." This allows relevant parties to participate in the inquiry and present their perspectives.

The power of the Minister to conduct inquiries is also outlined in Section 248(1), which states that the Minister
"...may, (a) for any of the purposes of this Part, cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment; and (b) appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry." This highlights the government's authority to investigate matters related to employment.

question: What happens after an inquiry into a member's conduct is completed, and what actions can be taken as a result?
answer:
## Outcomes and Actions Following an Inquiry

Here's a breakdown of what happens after an inquiry into a member's conduct, based on the provided documents:

### 1. Investigation Report and Recommendations

The primary outcome of an inquiry is the creation of an investigator's report. This report should include recommendations aimed at preventing similar occurrences in the future. 

>
"The investigator’s report should contain recommendations on  methods of eliminating or minimizing the risk of a similar occurrence in the  future."

This indicates that the report isn't just about assigning blame but also about identifying systemic issues and suggesting corrective actions.

### 2. No Automatic Appeal Process

According to the documents, there is no automatic appeal process if an employer is dissatisfied with the investigator's report or the way the investigation was conducted.

>
"As such, there is no appeal process under the Code or Regulations if:  you are not satisfied with the conclusions or  recommendations in the investigator’s report, or  you believe the investigation was flawed..."

However, the documents do outline a potential avenue for recourse.

### 3. Judicial Review

If concerns remain after communicating with the employer, an employee may be able to request a judicial review of the investigation by the Federal Court.

>
"If your concerns are not resolved, you may be able to  request a judicial review of the investigation by the Federal Court, within 30  days of receiving the investigator’s report."

It's important to note that this process is not prescribed by the Regulations, and legal counsel should be consulted.

### 4. Head's Investigation and Decisions (CLC-129)

In cases where the Head conducts an investigation, the outcome involves a decision based on the findings.

>
"The Head shall, on completion of an investigation made under subsection (1), make one of the decisions referred to in paragraphs 128(13)(a) to (c) and shall immediately give written notification of the decision to the employer and the employee."

These decisions can range from confirming the existence of a danger to issuing directions for corrective action. If the Head makes a decision related to a danger, the employee may not be able to continue refusing to use equipment or perform tasks, but they can appeal the decision to the Board within 10 days.

### 5. Continuation of Work During Investigation

During the investigation, the employer may require the employee to remain at a safe location or assign alternative work.

>
"If the employee has exercised their right under subsection (1.3), the employer may, during the investigation and until the Head has issued a decision, require that the employee concerned remain at a safe location near the place in respect of which the investigation is being made or assign the employee reasonable alternative work..."

This ensures safety while the investigation is ongoing.

### 6. Potential for Further Action (CLC-12.07)

The Minister has several options upon receiving a request for an inquiry, including referring the matter for mediation or requesting a formal inquiry by the Governor in Council.

>
"On receipt of the request, the Minister may take one or more of the following measures: (a) obtain, in an informal and expeditious manner, any information that the Minister considers necessary; (b) refer the matter for mediation, where the Minister is satisfied that the issues in relation to the request may be appropriately resolved by mediation; (c) request the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08; or (d) advise the Chairperson that the Minister considers that it is not necessary to take further measures under this section."

This suggests that the inquiry itself is a significant action, and the outcome can lead to further steps depending on the findings.

question: What are the requirements for determining a matter that comes before the Board, and who can determine such matters?
answer:
## Determining Matters Before the Board: Requirements and Authority

### Determining the Wishes of the Majority of Employees

Section 17 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process for determining the wishes of the majority of employees in a unit when required by the Board.
"Section 17 Where the Board is required, in connection with any application made under this Part, to determine the wishes of the majority of the employees in a unit, it shall determine those wishes as of the date of the filing of the application or as of such other date as the Board considers appropriate."

This indicates that the Board has the authority to determine the wishes of the majority of employees. The determination can be made either on the date the application is filed or on a later date deemed appropriate by the Board.

### Determination by Panel Chairperson in Case of Member Incapacity

Section 14.1 addresses the scenario where a member of a panel representing employees or employers becomes incapacitated or dies.
"Section 14.1 In the event of the death or incapacity of a member of a panel formed under subsection 14(1) who represents either employees or employers, the chairperson of the panel may determine any matter that was before the panel and the chairperson’s decision is deemed to be the decision of the panel."

This section clarifies that in such instances, the Chairperson of the panel assumes the authority to determine matters that were before the panel. The Chairperson's decision is considered equivalent to the decision of the entire panel.

### Board's Authority to Decide Without Oral Hearing

Section 16.1 grants the Board the power to make decisions without holding an oral hearing.
"Section 16.1 The Board may decide any matter before it without holding an oral hearing."

This suggests that the Board has the discretion to determine matters without a formal oral hearing process, implying that the requirements for determination may vary depending on the specific circumstances.

### Board's Role in Successor Rights and Obligations

Section 46 outlines the Board's responsibility in determining questions related to successor rights and obligations.
"Section 46 The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business."

This indicates that the Board is empowered to determine questions related to business transactions, including whether a business has been sold or undergone a change in activity.

question: What happens if a member of a panel, representing either employees or employers, dies or becomes incapacitated, and how are decisions made in such cases?
answer:
## Panel Member Death or Incapacity and Decision-Making

### Section 14.1: Determination by Chairperson
"In the event of the death or incapacity of a member of a panel formed under subsection 14(1) who represents either employees or employers, the chairperson of the panel may determine any matter that was before the panel and the chairperson’s decision is deemed to be the decision of the panel."

This section directly addresses the scenario of a panel member's death or incapacity. It clarifies that the chairperson of the panel has the authority to make a determination on any matter pending before the panel.  The significance of this is that the panel's work is not halted by the loss of a member. The chairperson effectively steps in to ensure the continuation of the panel's function.

### Section 14.2: Decision-Making Process After Incapacity
"Section 14.2 (1) A decision made by a majority of the members of a panel or, where there is no majority, by the chairperson of the panel is a decision of the Board."

This section outlines the process for making decisions after a panel member's death or incapacity. It states that a decision can be made either by a majority of the remaining panel members or, if no majority exists, by the chairperson. Crucially, it emphasizes that a decision made under either of these circumstances is considered a decision of the Board. This ensures that the panel's decisions retain the authority and weight of the Board's decisions.

### Section 14.2 (2): Time Limit for Decision
"(2) If a decision is to be made under this Part, the panel shall make it and give notice of it to the parties no later than 90 days after the day on which the panel reserved the decision or within any further period that may be determined by the Chairperson."

This subsection sets a time limit for the panel to make and notify the parties of its decision. The deadline is 90 days from the date the panel reserved the decision, or any extended period determined by the chairperson. This ensures a timely resolution of matters before the panel, even in the event of a member's death or incapacity.

question: What types of matters can the Board make regulations about in order to perform its duties under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Section 15 of the Canada Labour Code: Board Regulations

### General Authority for Regulations

Section 15 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Board broad authority to make regulations of general application. This authority is intended to assist the Board in properly performing its duties under the Act. The section states:
"...any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act." This broad language indicates that the Board's regulatory powers are not limited to specific areas but extend to anything that helps it fulfill its responsibilities.

### Specific Areas of Regulation

The section then lists a number of specific areas where the Board can make regulations. These include:

#### Pre-hearing Procedures and Hearings
"(a) the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings; (a.1) the use of means of telecommunication that permit the parties and the Board or its members to communicate simultaneously for pre-hearing conferences, hearings and Board meetings..."

This indicates the Board can regulate how its proceedings are conducted, including the use of technology for communication.

#### Collective Bargaining
"(b) the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining; (c) the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units; (d) the conduct of representation votes..."

The Board can establish rules for determining bargaining units and for conducting representation votes.

#### Certification of Trade Unions
"(c) the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units; (d) the conduct of representation votes; (e) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application from the trade union for certification in respect of the same or substantially the same unit..."

The Board can regulate the certification process for trade unions.

#### Evidence and Information
"(k) the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it..."

The Board can regulate how evidence is presented in proceedings.

#### Other Incidental Matters
"(q) any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act."

This final point reinforces the Board's broad regulatory power, allowing it to address any other matters that are necessary for it to effectively carry out its duties.

In essence, Section 15 empowers the Board to create detailed rules and procedures to facilitate its work in various aspects of labour relations, ensuring efficiency and fairness in its operations.

question: What types of assistance can the Board, its members, or external adjudicators provide to parties involved in a dispute under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Assistance Provided by the Board and Adjudicators

### General Power to Assist in Resolving Disputes

Section 15.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general power of the Board, its members, external adjudicators, and authorized employees of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada to assist parties in resolving disputes. This assistance can be provided at any stage of a proceeding and through any means deemed appropriate by the Board, provided the parties agree.
"The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled."

This indicates a flexible approach to dispute resolution, allowing for various forms of assistance as long as both parties consent. The Board's power to determine unresolved issues remains intact, ensuring that the assistance provided does not override the Board's authority to make final decisions.

### Declaratory Opinions

Section 15.1(2) grants the Board the authority to issue declaratory opinions upon application by an employer or a trade union.
"The Board, on application by an employer or a trade union, may give declaratory opinions."

This allows parties to seek clarification from the Board regarding their rights and obligations under the Canada Labour Code, potentially preventing disputes from escalating. These opinions are not binding but provide guidance on the interpretation of the Code.
