question: Under what conditions can the Board revoke the certification of a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit or declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit?
answer:
## Conditions for Revocation of Certification or Declaration of Inability to Represent

The Canada Labour Code outlines several conditions under which the Board can revoke the certification of a trade union as the bargaining agent or declare that a union is not entitled to represent employees in a bargaining unit. These conditions are detailed across multiple sections of the code.

### Revocation Based on a Motion by Employees, Employer, or Another Union

Section 40(1) states that
"...any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification." This indicates that a union's certification can be challenged at any time if fraud is alleged.

### Revocation Based on Lack of Employee Support

Section 39(1) specifies that
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit." This section highlights that if a majority of employees no longer desire the union's representation, the Board can revoke certification.

### Revocation Based on Evidence Not Presented During Certification Proceedings

Section 40(2) elaborates on the conditions for revocation based on fraud. It states that
"On receipt of an application under subsection (1) in respect of a trade union certification as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, the Board shall, by order, revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the Board is satisfied that the evidence in support of the application (a) was not and could not, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, have been presented to it in the certification proceeding; and (b) is such that the Board would have refused to certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the evidence had been presented to it in the certification proceeding." This means that if evidence of fraud was not presented during the initial certification process, and if that evidence would have led to a refusal of certification, the Board can revoke the certification.

### Revocation Based on Failure to Make Reasonable Efforts to Bargain

Section 39(2) adds a condition to the revocation process. It states,
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit." This indicates that the Board will not revoke certification solely based on the absence of a collective agreement if the union has made reasonable efforts to negotiate.

### Revocation Based on a Declaration of Inability to Represent

Section 42(1) states that
"Where the Board makes an order under section 39, subsection 40(2) or section 41 revoking the certification of a trade union or council of trade unions, or declaring that a trade union is not entitled to represent the employees in a bargaining unit..." this signifies that the Board can declare a union is not entitled to represent employees. This can occur as a result of a revocation order or a declaration made under other sections of the code.

question: Under what circumstances can a trade union's certification as a bargaining agent be revoked?
answer:
## Revocation of Trade Union Certification

### Section 42 of the Canada Labour Code
"Section 42 Where the Board makes an order under section 39, subsection 40(2) or section 41 revoking the certification of a trade union or council of trade unions, or declaring that a trade union is not entitled to represent the employees in a bargaining unit..."

This section outlines the primary circumstances under which a trade union's certification can be revoked. It explicitly states that the Board can revoke certification through orders made under sections 39, 40(2), or 41 of the Canada Labour Code. These sections address situations such as a failure to fulfill duties or a lack of support from the employees.

### Section 38 of the Canada Labour Code
"If a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Board for an order revoking the certification of that trade union."

This section allows employees to petition the Board for revocation of a trade union's certification. An employee can apply for revocation if they believe the certification was improperly granted or if the union is no longer representing the employees' interests.

### Section 40 of the Canada Labour Code
"Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification."

This section provides another avenue for revocation, specifically when fraud is alleged in the certification process. Employees, employers, or other unions who believe the certification was obtained through fraudulent means can apply to the Board for revocation.

### Section 39 of the Canada Labour Code
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."

This section allows the Board to revoke certification if it determines that a majority of employees no longer wish to be represented by the union. This can be determined through a representation vote or other means deemed appropriate by the Board.

In summary, a trade union's certification as a bargaining agent can be revoked due to:

*   Orders made by the Board under sections 39, 40(2), or 41 of the Canada Labour Code.
*   Applications by employees alleging improper certification.
*   Applications by employees, employers, or other unions alleging fraud in the certification process.
*   The Board's determination that a majority of employees no longer wish to be represented by the union.

question: Under what circumstances can an application be made to revoke the certification of a council of trade unions as a bargaining agent?
answer:
## Revocation of Certification of a Council of Trade Unions

### Section 41(1) - General Grounds for Application
"Where a council of trade unions has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, in addition to any circumstances in which an application for revocation of the certification of the council of trade unions may be made pursuant to section 38 or subsection 40(1), any employee in the bargaining unit, the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit or a trade union that forms part of the council of trade unions may apply to the Board for revocation of the certification on the ground that the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions."

This section outlines the circumstances under which an application can be made to revoke the certification of a council of trade unions. It states that an application can be made by
"...any employee in the bargaining unit, the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit or a trade union that forms part of the council of trade unions..." The grounds for such an application are that
"...the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions." This indicates that the application is not limited to specific reasons like fraud, but can be based on a broader assessment that the council is no longer eligible to hold the certification.

### Section 38(1) - Application Based on Majority Wishes
"If a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Board for an order revoking the certification of that trade union."

While this section primarily addresses individual trade unions, it is relevant as it establishes the principle that a majority of employees' wishes can be a basis for revoking certification. This principle could potentially apply to a council of trade unions if a majority of the employees no longer wish to be represented by the council.

### Section 40(1) - Application Based on Fraud
"Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification."

This section provides another ground for application, specifically alleging that the certification was obtained through fraud. This applies to a council of trade unions in the same manner as it applies to a single trade union.

### Section 39(1) - Application Based on Lack of Employee Support
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."

This section states that if the Board is satisfied that a majority of employees no longer wish to be represented by the bargaining agent, the certification can be revoked. This applies to a council of trade unions as well.

In summary, an application to revoke the certification of a council of trade unions can be made by employees, employers, or affiliated trade unions if the council no longer meets certification requirements, if fraud was involved in obtaining the certification, or if a majority of the employees no longer wish to be represented by the council.

question: What happens to a collective agreement between a trade union and an employer if the Board makes an order revoking the trade union's certification, and what restrictions are placed on the employer?
answer:
## Effect of Certification Revocation on Collective Agreements and Employer Bargaining

### Section 42: Effect of Revocation
"Where the Board makes an order under section 39, subsection 40(2) or section 41 revoking the certification of a trade union or council of trade unions, or declaring that a trade union is not entitled to represent the employees in a bargaining unit..."

This section directly addresses the consequences of the Board's decision to revoke a trade union's certification. It states that any collective agreement between the union and the employer
"...that applies to the bargaining unit ceases to have effect from the time the order is made or from such later time as the Board considers appropriate..." This means that upon the revocation of certification, the existing collective agreement is no longer legally binding.

### Restrictions on Employer Bargaining
"(b) the employer shall not bargain collectively, or enter into a collective agreement with the trade union or council of trade unions, for a period of one year from the date of the order, unless the trade union or council of trade unions is certified by the Board under this Part during that period as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit comprised of employees of the employer."

Following the revocation of certification, the employer is restricted from engaging in collective bargaining with the previously certified union for a period of one year. This restriction is in place
"...unless the trade union or council of trade unions is certified by the Board under this Part during that period as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit comprised of employees of the employer." This implies that the employer can resume collective bargaining only if a new union is certified within the one-year period. The employer is essentially prevented from continuing to bargain with a union that no longer has the legal authority to represent the employees.

question: What happens to the rights, privileges, and duties of a trade union when it is succeeded by another trade union due to a merger, amalgamation, or transfer of jurisdiction?
answer:
## Successor Rights and Obligations: Mergers, etc., of Trade Unions - Section 43

### Acquisition of Rights, Privileges, and Duties

Section 43(1) directly addresses the scenario of a trade union succeeding another due to a merger, amalgamation, or transfer of jurisdiction. It states:
"Where, by reason of a merger or amalgamation of trade unions or a transfer of jurisdiction among trade unions, a trade union succeeds another trade union that, at the time of the merger, amalgamation or transfer of jurisdiction, is a bargaining agent, the successor shall be deemed to have acquired the rights, privileges and duties of its predecessor, whether under a collective agreement or otherwise."

This means that if one trade union merges with or takes over the jurisdiction of another that is already a bargaining agent, the new union automatically inherits all the rights, privileges, and duties of the previous union. This includes obligations arising from collective agreements. The phrase "successor shall be deemed to have acquired" indicates a legal presumption, simplifying the transfer of responsibility.

### Board Determination

Section 43(2) outlines the role of the Board in situations where questions arise regarding the rights, privileges, and duties of a trade union following a merger, amalgamation, or transfer of jurisdiction. It states:
"Where, on a merger or amalgamation of trade unions or a transfer of jurisdiction among trade unions, any question arises concerning the rights, privileges and duties of a trade union under this Part or under a collective agreement in respect of a bargaining unit or an employee therein, the Board, on application to it by a trade union affected by the merger, amalgamation or transfer of jurisdiction, shall determine what rights, privileges and duties have been acquired or are retained."

This provision ensures that any uncertainties or disputes regarding the transfer of rights and duties are resolved by the Board. The Board can be petitioned by any trade union affected by the merger, ensuring a fair and impartial determination.

### Board Inquiry

Section 43(3) further clarifies the Board's authority in determining these rights and duties. It states:
"Before determining, pursuant to subsection (2), what rights, privileges and duties of a trade union have been acquired or are retained, the Board may make such inquiry or direct that such representation votes be taken as it..."

This allows the Board to conduct investigations and take necessary steps, such as holding representation votes, to ensure a thorough and accurate assessment of the situation. This ensures that the determination is based on all relevant information and reflects the interests of the affected parties.

question: What happens to the labour relations of employees when a business is sold, particularly in terms of their bargaining agent and collective agreements?
answer:
## Section 44(2)(a) - Continuation of Bargaining Agent
"Where an employer sells a business, (a) a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent..."

This section directly addresses the continuity of the bargaining agent when a business is sold. It explicitly states that the existing trade union representing the employees in the sold business automatically retains its status as the bargaining agent for those employees after the sale. This ensures that the employees have a consistent representative to advocate for their interests.

## Section 44(2)(c) - Binding Nature of Collective Agreements
"...the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business..."

This part of Section 44(2) clarifies that the buyer of the business inherits the existing collective agreements.  The new owner is obligated to adhere to the terms and conditions outlined in any collective agreements that were in effect for the employees at the time of the sale. This protects the employees' rights and benefits as established through their collective bargaining agreements.

## Section 44(2)(d) - Continuation of Pending Proceedings
"...the person to whom the business is sold becomes a party to any proceeding taken under this Part that is pending on the date on which the business was sold and that affects the employees employed in the business or their bargaining agent."

This provision ensures that any ongoing labour-related legal proceedings are not disrupted by the sale of the business. The new owner becomes involved in any existing legal actions concerning the employees or their bargaining agent, ensuring continuity and fairness in the resolution of such matters.

## Section 47.1(1)(a) - Continuation of Collective Agreements and Arbıtral Awards After Deletion
"...a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..."

This section applies when a portion of the federal public administration becomes part of a corporation or business. question: What is the role of the Board in the event of a sale or change of activity affecting employees' collective bargaining units?
answer:
## The Board's Role in Sales or Changes of Activity Affecting Collective Bargaining Units

The Canada Labour Code outlines the Board's significant role when a sale or change of activity affects employees' collective bargaining units. This role primarily revolves around determining the appropriate bargaining unit structure and ensuring continuity of employee rights.

### Determining Appropriate Bargaining Units

Section 45 states:
"In the case of a sale or change of activity referred to in section 44, the Board may, on application by the employer or any trade union affected, determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that the Board has the authority to review and redefine bargaining units when a business is sold or undergoes a change in activity. This determination is made upon application from either the employer or a trade union impacted by the change.

Section 46 further clarifies this by stating:
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business." This reinforces the Board's responsibility to assess the impact of sales and changes in activity on bargaining unit definitions.

### Reviewing and Implementing Bargaining Unit Changes

Section 18.1 outlines the Board's process for reviewing bargaining unit structures. It states:
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining." This demonstrates the Board's proactive role in ensuring bargaining units remain relevant and effective.

Furthermore, Section 18.1(2) details the Board's responsibilities when reviewing bargaining units. It states:
"If the Board reviews, pursuant to subsection (1) or section 35 or 45, the structure of the bargaining units, the Board (a) must allow the parties to come to an agreement, within a period that the Board considers reasonable, with respect to the determination of bargaining units and any questions arising from the review; and (b) may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement." This highlights the Board's role in facilitating agreement between parties and, if necessary, issuing orders to implement the agreed-upon changes.

### Addressing Disagreements and Making Determinations

Section 18.1(3) addresses situations where the parties cannot reach an agreement. It states:
"If the Board is of the opinion that the agreement reached by the parties would not lead to the creation of units appropriate for collective bargaining or if the parties do not agree on certain issues within the period that the Board considers reasonable, the Board determines any question that arises and makes any orders it considers appropriate in the circumstances." This emphasizes the Board's ultimate authority to make decisions regarding bargaining unit structure when parties fail to reach a consensus.

In summary, the Board plays a crucial role in ensuring that employees' collective bargaining units remain appropriate following a sale or change of activity. This involves determining the appropriate unit structure, facilitating agreement between parties, and issuing orders when necessary to ensure fair and effective collective bargaining arrangements.

question: What is the role of the Board in relation to questions that arise regarding business sales or changes in business activity under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## The Board's Role in Business Sales and Activity Changes

### Section 46: Board Determination of Questions Arising from Business Transfers

Section 46 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the Board's responsibility concerning questions related to business sales and changes in business activity.

**Board's Authority to Determine Questions
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business."

This section clearly establishes that the Board has the authority to resolve disputes and make determinations regarding business sales and changes in business activity. This includes determining whether a business has been sold, if there has been a change in the nature of the business, and identifying the purchaser in the event of a sale. This power is directly linked to Section 44, which defines "business" and outlines the consequences of business sales and changes of activity for trade unions and employees. The Board's role is to provide clarity and resolve ambiguities that may arise from these transactions.



### Section 44: Consequences of Business Sales and Activity Changes

While Section 46 focuses on the Board's determination of questions, Section 44 details the consequences of business sales and changes in activity. This section provides context for the types of questions the Board will address.

**Continuity of Union Representation
"(a) a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent; (b) a trade union that made application for certification in respect of any employees employed in the business before the date on which the business is sold may, subject to this Part, be certified by the Board as their bargaining agent; (c) the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business; and (d) the person to whom the business is sold becomes a party to any proceeding taken under this Part that is pending on the date on which the business was sold and that affects the employees employed in the business or their bargaining agent."

This excerpt from Section 44 highlights that even after a business sale, the existing trade union often retains its bargaining rights. The Board is involved in ensuring this continuity and resolving any disputes related to it.

**Board's Role in Resolving Disputes
"(g) the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board; (g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure..."

This section indicates that the Board is empowered to hear and determine any questions, disputes, or appeals that arise in connection with business sales or changes in business activity. This includes resolving issues related to the transfer of collective agreements, the certification of unions, and other related matters.

question: What happens to a collective agreement or arbitral award when a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which the Part applies?
answer:
## Section 47: Successor Rights and Obligations

### Impact of Corporate Transformation on Collective Agreements and Awards

Section 47(1) addresses the fate of collective agreements and arbitral awards when a portion of the federal public administration transitions into a corporation or business covered by the relevant part of the Canada Labour Code. 

The section states:
"...a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..."

This means that existing collective agreements and arbitral awards remain in effect even after the administrative portion becomes part of a corporation or business. The continuation is subject to certain conditions outlined in subsections (3) to (7). This ensures that the rights and obligations established by the previous agreement are not automatically voided by the change in organizational structure.

### Application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act

Furthermore, the section clarifies that the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award in this scenario. 

The text specifies:
"...and (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award."

This ensures that the legal framework governing the collective agreement or award remains consistent despite the change in administrative structure. The Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act provides the rules and procedures for interpreting and applying the agreement, ensuring fairness and predictability.

## Successor Rights and Obligations: Transition from Federal Public Administration to Corporation/Business

### Section 47.1 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 47.1 addresses the continuation of collective agreements and arbitral awards when employees transition from the federal public administration to a corporation or business.
"Section 47.1 Where, before the deletion or severance referred to in subsection 47(1), notice to bargain collectively has been given in respect of a collective agreement or arbitral award binding on employees of a corporation or business who, immediately before the deletion or severance, were part of the federal public administration..."

This section clarifies that if a notice to bargain collectively was given before the transition, the terms and conditions of employment outlined in the existing collective agreement or arbitral award continue to be in effect.
"...collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7)..."

This means that the existing agreement remains valid until its expiration date, subject to certain conditions outlined in subsequent subsections.

### Section 47 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 47 further elaborates on the continuation of collective agreements and arbitral awards during the transition.
"Section 47 (1) Where the name of any portion of the federal public administration specified from time to time in Schedule I, IV or V to the Financial Administration Act is deleted and that portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which this Part applies, or where a portion of the federal public administration included in another portion of the federal public administration specified in those Schedules is severed from the portion in which it was included and established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business..."

This section states that when a portion of the federal public administration is transferred to a corporation or business, the existing collective agreement or arbitral award remains in effect.
"...collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in..."

This ensures that employees do not immediately lose their established terms and conditions of employment upon the transition.

### Section 47(2) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 47(2) provides a mechanism for certification of a new bargaining unit.
"(2) A trade union may apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for the employees affected by a collective agreement or arbitral award referred to in subsection (1), but may so apply only during a period in which an application for certification of a trade union is authorized to be made under section 24."

This allows the union representing the former public administration employees to seek certification as the bargaining agent for the employees within the new corporation or business. This ensures that the employees have a representative to advocate for their interests.

question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1?
answer:
## Governor in Council Exclusion of Federal Public Administration from Sections 47 and 47.1

### Section 47.2: General Authority for Exclusion

Section 47.2 grants the Governor in Council the authority to exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1. This exclusion can occur when the portion of the federal public administration is deleted or severed, as described in subsection 47(1).

>
"The Governor in Council may, by order, exclude from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1 any portion of the federal public administration that is deleted or severed as described in subsection 47(1) where the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for that portion of the federal public administration, is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to do so."

This indicates that the Governor in Council's power to exclude is not absolute. It is contingent upon a specific set of conditions.

### Conditions for Exclusion

The exclusion is subject to the following conditions:

1.  **Deletion or Severance:** The portion of the federal public administration must have been deleted or severed, as defined in subsection 47(1).
2.  **Ministerial Recommendation:** The Governor in Council must act upon the recommendation of the Minister.
3.  **Consultation:** Prior to making the decision, the Minister must consult with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for the portion of the federal public administration in question.
4.  **Public Interest:** The Governor in Council must be of the opinion that the exclusion is in the public interest.

Therefore, the Governor in Council can exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1, but only if that portion has been deleted or severed, and this decision is made after consultation with relevant ministers and is deemed to be in the public interest.

question: What are the requirements for an employer who takes over providing services from a previous contractor under a contract or arrangement?
answer:
## Successive Contracts for Services - Requirements for New Employers

### Section 47.3 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 47.3 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the obligations of an employer who takes over providing services from a previous contractor. The core requirement is ensuring that employees continue to receive at least the same level of remuneration as their counterparts under the previous contract.

### Remuneration Requirements
"An employer who succeeds a previous contractor as the provider of services, in accordance with a contract or other arrangement, must pay to the employees providing the services under that contract or arrangement remuneration not less than that which the employees of the previous contractor who provided the same or substantially similar services were entitled to receive under the terms of a collective agreement to which this Part applied."

This section mandates that the new employer must not reduce the wages or benefits of the employees they are taking over. The remuneration must be "not less than" what the employees of the previous contractor were receiving under any applicable collective agreement. This ensures that employees are not disadvantaged when a change in service providers occurs.

### Scope of Application

The requirements of Section 47.3 apply to situations where an employer takes over providing services under a contract or arrangement, as defined in Section 47.3(1). This includes scenarios where the previous contractor provided services at an airport, provided prescribed services in a prescribed industry, or provided prescribed services at a prescribed location in a prescribed industry.

### Collective Agreements

The obligation to pay at least the same remuneration is tied to the terms of a collective agreement. This means that if a collective agreement exists for the employees of the previous contractor, the new employer must adhere to the terms of that agreement.

In essence, Section 47.3 aims to protect the employment terms of workers when a change in service providers occurs, ensuring that they are not negatively impacted financially.

question: What can a certified bargaining agent or an employer do to initiate collective bargaining when no collective agreement is in force?
answer:
## Initiating Collective Bargaining When No Collective Agreement is in Force

Here's a breakdown of what a certified bargaining agent or an employer can do to initiate collective bargaining when no collective agreement is in force, based on the provided Canada Labour Code sections.

### Section 24 (1)(b) - Application for Certification
"Subject to subsection (3), an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit may be made (a) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and no trade union has been certified under this Part..."

This section outlines that a trade union can apply for certification at any time when no collective agreement is currently in effect. This is the initial step for a union seeking to become the bargaining agent.

### Section 24 (2)(c) - Application for Certification
"...collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force but a trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, after the expiration of twelve months from the date of that certification or, with the consent of the Board, at any earlier time..."

This section specifies that even if a collective agreement is in place, a certified union can still initiate bargaining after twelve months from the date of certification, or earlier with the Board's consent. This allows for periodic renegotiation of existing agreements.

### Section 36 (2)(b) - Effect of Certification
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..."

This section clarifies that once a union is certified, it has the exclusive authority to bargain collectively. This implies that the union is the entity that initiates and conducts collective bargaining.

### Section 36 (2)(b) - Effect of Certification
"...the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto..."

This section further reinforces the union's role as the primary bargaining agent. It states that the union is substituted as a party to any existing collective agreement, effectively taking over the bargaining responsibilities.

### Section 36 (2)(b) - Effect of Certification
"...the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

This section confirms the union's status as the designated bargaining agent for all relevant purposes.

### Employer's Role

While the certified union has the primary role in initiating collective bargaining, the employer is also involved.
"Where an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit is made in accordance with this section, no employer of employees in the unit shall, after notification that the application has been made, alter the rates of pay, any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of such employees until (a) the application has been withdrawn by the trade union or dismissed by the Board, or (b) thirty days have elapsed after the day on which the Board certifies the trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit, except pursuant to a collective agreement or with the consent of the Board."

This section indicates that an employer cannot alter terms and conditions of employment after being notified of a certification application until the application is withdrawn, dismissed, or the union is certified. This implies that the employer must wait for the union to be officially recognized before engaging in collective bargaining.

In summary, a certified bargaining agent (the union) initiates collective bargaining by applying for certification when no agreement is in force, or by initiating negotiations after a period of time has passed since certification. The employer's role is to refrain from altering terms and conditions of employment during the certification process and to engage in bargaining once the union is officially certified.

question: What are the requirements for a party to a collective agreement to initiate collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing, revising, or entering into a new collective agreement?
answer:
## Initiating Collective Bargaining for Renewal, Revision, or New Agreement

### Section 48: General Requirement to Initiate Bargaining
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

This section outlines the fundamental requirement for initiating collective bargaining when no existing agreement covers the employees. Either the bargaining agent or the employer can initiate the process by providing notice to the other party. This establishes the initial trigger for collective bargaining.

### Section 49: Renewal, Revision, or New Agreement - Notice Requirements

**(1)
"Either party to a collective agreement may, within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement, by notice, require the other party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This section details the specific timeframe for initiating bargaining related to an existing collective agreement.  It states that
"Either party to a collective agreement may, within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement, by notice, require the other party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement." This means that bargaining must be initiated within a specific window before the current agreement expires, or according to the terms outlined within the existing collective agreement itself.

**(2)
"Where a collective agreement provides that any provision of the collective agreement may be revised during the term of the collective agreement, a party entitled to do so by the collective agreement may, by notice, require the other party to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of revising the provision."

This subsection addresses the possibility of revising specific provisions within an existing collective agreement. It clarifies that if the collective agreement itself allows for revisions during its term, a party can initiate bargaining to address those specific provisions. This provides a mechanism for making adjustments to the agreement without requiring a complete renegotiation.

question: What are the obligations of the bargaining agent and the employer once notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations)?
answer:
## Obligations After Notice to Bargain Collectively

### Section 50: Duty to Bargain in Good Faith

Section 50 outlines the immediate obligations of both the bargaining agent and the employer once notice to bargain collectively has been given.
"Where notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part, (a) the bargaining agent and the employer, without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement..."

This section emphasizes the requirement for both parties to initiate bargaining promptly. The timeframe is set at twenty days, although parties can agree to a different schedule. Crucially, it mandates that bargaining must occur "in good faith." This means both sides must approach the negotiations with a sincere willingness to reach an agreement.

### Section 50: Prohibition on Altering Terms and Conditions

Furthermore, Section 50 restricts the employer's ability to unilaterally alter terms and conditions of employment during the bargaining process.
"(b) the employer shall not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the bargaining agent consents to the alteration of such a term or condition, or such a right or privilege."

This provision protects the employees' interests by preventing the employer from changing conditions before a collective agreement is reached. The employer can only make changes with the bargaining agent's consent, ensuring that any alterations are negotiated and agreed upon.

question: Under what conditions do sections 52, 54, and 55 of the Canada Labour Code not apply to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement in the context of a technological change?
answer:
## Conditions for Non-Application of Sections 52, 54, and 55

Sections 52, 54, and 55 of the Canada Labour Code do not apply to an employer and a bargaining agent bound by a collective agreement under specific circumstances related to technological change. These conditions are outlined in Section 51(2) of the Canada Labour Code.

### 1. Notice Given Prior to Collective Agreement or Within Specified Timeframes
"Sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, in respect of a technological change, to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement where (a) the employer has given to the bargaining agent a notice in writing of the technological change that is substantially in accordance with subsection 52(2), (i) prior to the day on which the employer and the bargaining agent entered into the collective agreement, if the notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into that collective agreement was given pursuant to section 48, or (ii) not later than the last day on which notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the collective agreement could have been given pursuant to subsection 49(1), if the notice was given under that subsection..."

This condition states that if the employer provides a written notice of the technological change that substantially aligns with the requirements of Section 52(2), and this notice is given either before the collective agreement is signed (if the notice to commence bargaining was given under Section 48) or by the last possible date for such a notice (if given under Section 49(1)), then Sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply. This suggests that early and compliant notification can preempt the need for these sections to govern the change.

### 2. Collective Agreement Provisions for Negotiation and Settlement
"(b) the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement..."

This condition allows for the non-application of Sections 52, 54, and 55 if the collective agreement itself includes procedures for negotiating and resolving issues related to technological changes. This implies that the parties have already established a framework within their agreement to address such changes, rendering the statutory requirements of Sections 52, 54, and 55 unnecessary.

### 3. Collective Agreement Provisions for Employee Adjustment and Exclusion of Statutory Requirements
"...or (c) the collective agreement contains provisions that (i) are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and (ii) specify that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent."

This condition provides a direct exclusion of Sections 52, 54, and 55 if the collective agreement contains provisions designed to help employees adapt to the technological change and explicitly states that these sections do not apply during the agreement's term. This indicates that the parties have proactively addressed the potential impact of the technological change within the collective agreement itself.

question: What are the requirements for an employer bound by a collective agreement to implement a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees?
answer:
## Requirements for Implementing Technological Change

### Section 52: Notice of Technological Change

Section 52 outlines the specific requirements for an employer bound by a collective agreement to notify the bargaining agent of a technological change. 

**Timing of Notice:
"An employer who is bound by a collective agreement and who proposes to effect a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of the employer’s employees to whom the collective agreement applies shall give notice of the technological change to the bargaining agent bound by the collective agreement at least one hundred and twenty days prior to the date on which the technological change is to be effected."

This indicates that the employer must provide notice at least 120 days before implementing the change.

**Content of the Notice:
"The notice referred to in subsection (1) shall be in writing and shall state (a) the nature of the technological change; (b) the date on which the employer proposes to effect the technological change; (c) the approximate number and type of employees likely to be affected by the technological change; (d) the effect that the technological change is likely to have on the terms and conditions or security of employment of the employees affected; and (e) such other information as is required by the regulations made pursuant to subsection (4)."

The notice must be in writing and include detailed information about the technological change, including its nature, implementation date, the number and type of affected employees, and the anticipated impact on their terms and conditions of employment. Additionally, the employer may be required to include other information as specified by regulations.

**Providing Additional Information Upon Request:
"An employer who has given notice under subsection (1) to a bargaining agent shall, on request from the bargaining agent, provide the bargaining agent with a statement in writing setting out (a) a detailed description of the nature of the proposed technological change; (b) the names of the employees who will initially be likely to be affected by the proposed technological change; and (c) the rationale for the change."

The employer is obligated to provide further details, including a detailed description, names of initially affected employees, and the rationale behind the change, if requested by the bargaining agent.

### Section 52(4): Regulations
"The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Board, may make regulations (a) specifying the number of employees or the method of determining the number of employees that shall, in respect of any federal work, undertaking or business, be deemed to be “significant” for the purposes of subsections (1) and 54(2); and (b) requiring any information in addition to the information required by subsection (2) to be included in a notice of technological change."

This section allows the Governor in Council to create regulations that further define the requirements for the notice, including how "significant" numbers of employees are determined and what additional information must be included.

question: What can a bargaining agent do if they allege that an employer has failed to comply with the requirements related to technological changes, and what are the potential outcomes of such an action?
answer:
## Bargaining Agent's Actions Upon Alleged Non-Compliance with Technological Change Requirements

### Section 53: Application for Order Determining Alleged Non-Compliance

Section 53 outlines the procedure a bargaining agent can follow if they believe an employer has failed to comply with the requirements of sections 52, 54, and 55 regarding technological changes.

**Initiating the Application:
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."

This indicates that the bargaining agent must file an application with the Board within 30 days of becoming aware of the alleged non-compliance with Section 52. The Board can then investigate the matter.

### Potential Outcomes of the Application

Upon receiving the application, the Board has several options:

**1. Determining Non-Application of Sections 52, 54, and 55:
"On receipt of an application for an order determining the matters alleged under subsection (1) and after affording an opportunity for the parties to make representations, the Board may, by order, (a) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change..."

The Board can issue an order stating that sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply to the specific technological change in question. This would effectively dismiss the bargaining agent's concerns.

**2. Determining Application and Non-Compliance:
"...or (b) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52 in respect of the technological change."

The Board can also issue an order confirming that sections 52, 54, and 55 *do* apply and that the employer has indeed failed to comply with Section 52. This is a critical finding that triggers further actions.

### Consequences of Finding Non-Compliance

If the Board determines that the employer has failed to comply with Section 52, the Board has the power to take several actions:

**1. Directing Non-Proceeding with the Technological Change:
"(a) direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for such period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate..."

The Board can order the employer to halt the technological change for up to 120 days.

**2. Requiring Reinstatement of Displaced Employees:
"(b) require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change..."

The Board can order the employer to reinstate any employees who have been displaced due to the technological change.

**3. Requiring Reimbursement for Lost Pay:
"...and (c) where an employee is reinstated pursuant to paragraph (b), require the employer to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement."

If an employee is reinstated, the Board can order the employer to reimburse the employee for any lost wages incurred as a result of their displacement.

**4. Deemed Notice of Technological Change:
"(4) An order of the Board made under paragraph (2)(b) in respect of an employer is deemed to be a notice of technological change given by the employer pursuant to section 52, and the Board shall concurrently, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1)."

If the Board determines non-compliance and issues an order, that order is treated as if the employer had properly provided notice of the technological change as required by Section 52. This allows the bargaining agent to proceed with collective bargaining.



In summary, if a bargaining agent believes an employer has failed to comply with the requirements of technological change, they can apply to the Board. The Board can either dismiss the application or, if it finds non-compliance, order the employer to halt the change, reinstate displaced employees, reimburse lost wages, and effectively treat the employer's actions as proper notice of the technological change, thereby allowing for collective bargaining.

question: What recourse does a bargaining agent have when it receives notice of a technological change that may adversely affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees bound by a collective agreement?
answer:
## Recourse for Bargaining Agents Upon Receiving Notice of Technological Change

### Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain (Section 54)

Section 54 outlines the recourse available to a bargaining agent upon receiving notice of a technological change. It states:
"Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."

This section provides a direct avenue for the bargaining agent to initiate collective bargaining. The agent can apply to the Board within 30 days of receiving the notice of technological change to obtain permission to serve a notice to the employer to begin negotiations. The purpose of this collective bargaining is to either modify the existing collective agreement or add new provisions to address the impact of the technological change on employees' terms and conditions of employment.

### Board's Power to Grant Leave (Section 54(2))

Section 54(2) further clarifies the Board's role in this process. It states:
"Where the Board has received from a bargaining agent an application for an order under subsection (1), and it is satisfied that the technological change in respect of which the bargaining agent has received notice given pursuant to section 52 is likely, substantially and adversely, to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees to whom the collective agreement between the bargaining agent and the employer applies, the Board may, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection (1)."

This subsection empowers the Board to grant the bargaining agent leave to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining if it determines that the technological change is likely to have a significant and adverse impact on a substantial number of employees. This ensures that the Board can intervene to facilitate a fair and timely negotiation process when necessary.

In essence, upon receiving notice of a technological change, a bargaining agent can apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining. This allows the agent to proactively address the potential adverse effects of the change on employees' terms and conditions of employment through negotiation. The Board has the authority to grant this leave if it finds the technological change to be likely to substantially and adversely affect a significant number of employees.

question: What happens to an employer's ability to effect a technological change when a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1)?
answer:
## Impact of a Board Order Application on Technological Change

### Section 55: Conditions Precedent to Technological Change
"Where a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer in respect of whom the application is made shall not effect the technological change in respect of which the application is made until (a) the Board has made an order refusing to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining; or (b) the Board has made an order granting leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining and (i) an agreement has been reached as a result of collective bargaining, or (ii) the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

This section outlines the conditions that must be met before an employer can implement a technological change following an application to the Board. Essentially, the employer's ability to proceed with the change is put on hold. The employer cannot effect the technological change "until" one of two conditions is met: either the Board denies the bargaining agent's request for a notice to commence collective bargaining, or the Board grants the request and one of the specified conditions related to collective bargaining is fulfilled. This demonstrates a clear pause in the employer's ability to implement the change while the Board considers the application.

### Section 54: Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain
"Section 54 (1) Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."
"(2) Where the Board has received from a bargaining agent an application for an order under subsection (1), and it is satisfied that the technological change in respect of which the bargaining agent has received notice given pursuant to section 52 is likely, substantially and adversely, to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees to whom the collective agreement between the bargaining agent and the employer applies, the Board may, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection (1)."

These sections further elaborate on the process when a bargaining agent applies for an order to commence collective bargaining. The employer's ability to proceed with the technological change is directly linked to the Board's decision on whether to grant the bargaining agent leave to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining. If the Board grants the leave, the employer's ability to implement the change is further delayed until collective bargaining occurs or other specified conditions are met. The Board's assessment of the potential adverse impact on employees is a key factor in determining whether to grant the leave, highlighting the Board's role in protecting employee interests during technological change.

### Section 53: Application for Order Respecting Technological Change
"Section 53 (1) Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."
"(3) The Board may, in any order made under paragraph (2)(b), or by order made after consultation with the parties pending the making of any order under subsection (2), (a) direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for such period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate..."

This section provides another avenue for delaying the technological change. If a bargaining agent believes that sections 52, 54, and 55 apply and the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the agent can apply to the Board for an order. The Board has the power to order the employer to halt the technological change for up to 120 days. This demonstrates that the Board can directly intervene and prevent the employer from implementing the change while the matter is being investigated and resolved.

In summary, when a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer's ability to effect a technological change is significantly restricted. The employer cannot proceed until the Board either denies the bargaining agent's request or grants it, and even then, the employer's ability to implement the change may be further delayed depending on the outcome of collective bargaining or other conditions. The Board also has the power to directly order the employer to halt the technological change for a specified period.

question: What is required to be included in a collective agreement in Canada regarding the resolution of differences between parties, and what happens if the parties are unable to agree on an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson?
answer:
## Collective Agreement Dispute Resolution in Canada

### Mandatory Provisions for Resolving Differences

Section 57(1) of the Canada Labour Code mandates that
"Every collective agreement shall contain a provision for final settlement without stoppage of work, by arbitration or otherwise, of all differences between the parties to or employees bound by the collective agreement, concerning its interpretation, application, administration or alleged contravention." This means that any collective agreement in Canada *must* include a mechanism for resolving disputes. This mechanism can be arbitration or another agreed-upon method. The purpose of this provision is to ensure that differences are resolved without work stoppages.

### Procedures When Parties Cannot Agree on an Arbitrator or Chairperson

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific procedures when parties cannot agree on an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson.

**1. Initial Selection:
"Where any difference arises between parties to a collective agreement that does not contain a provision for final settlement of the difference as required by subsection (1), the difference shall, notwithstanding any provision of the collective agreement, be submitted by the parties for final settlement (a) to an arbitrator selected by the parties; or (b) where the parties are unable to agree on the selection of an arbitrator and either party makes a written request to the Minister to appoint an arbitrator, to an arbitrator appointed by the Minister after such inquiry, if any, as the Minister..."

This section details the initial process. If the collective agreement lacks a dispute resolution mechanism, the parties must first attempt to select an arbitrator. If they cannot agree, either party can request the Minister to appoint an arbitrator.

**2. Minister's Appointment:
"Where a collective agreement provides for final settlement, without stoppage of work, of differences described in subsection (1) by an arbitrator or arbitration board and the parties or their nominees are unable to agree on the selection of an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, as the case may be, either party or its nominee may, notwithstanding anything in the collective agreement, make a written request to the Minister to appoint an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, as the case may be."

If the collective agreement *does* provide for arbitration or an arbitration board, but the parties cannot agree on the chairperson, either party can request the Minister's appointment.

**3. Minister's Authority:
"On receipt of a written request under subsection (4), the Minister shall, after such inquiry, if any, as the Minister considers necessary, appoint an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, as the case may be."

The Minister has the authority to appoint an arbitrator or chairperson after receiving a written request and conducting a necessary inquiry.

**4. Appointment as per Agreement:
"Any person appointed or selected pursuant to subsection (2), (3) or (5) as an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson shall be deemed, for all purposes of this Part, to have been appointed pursuant to the collective agreement between the parties."

Regardless of how the arbitrator or chairperson is appointed (by the parties or the Minister), they are considered to have been appointed under the collective agreement. This ensures the process remains linked to the agreement.

question: What is the status of an arbitrator or arbitration board's decision under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Status of Arbitrator or Arbitration Board Decisions Under the Canada Labour Code

### Finality of Decisions

Section 58(1) of the Canada Labour Code states,
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This indicates that, generally, decisions made by arbitrators or arbitration boards are considered conclusive and binding. 

### Exceptions to Finality

However, the text acknowledges limited circumstances where a decision might be subject to review. Section 16(2) mentions that
"...a  process called judicial review (which is a review of the referee’s decision by a court) may be available if the  referee has made an error of  jurisdiction or failed to observe a principle of administrative fairness." This suggests that judicial review is not a standard avenue but is reserved for cases involving significant procedural errors or jurisdictional issues. The text further emphasizes the complexity and time constraints associated with seeking judicial review, advising consultation with a lawyer.

### No Court Review

Section 58(2) reinforces the finality of decisions by stating,
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain an arbitrator or arbitration board in any of their proceedings under this Part." This provision explicitly prohibits courts from interfering with the arbitrator's or arbitration board's processes.

### Decisions of Panels

Section 14.2(2) clarifies that a decision made by a majority of the members of a panel or, where there is no majority, by the chairperson of the panel is a decision of the Board. This means that decisions made by panels formed under the Canada Labour Code are considered decisions of the Board and are subject to the finality described above.

In summary, arbitrator or arbitration board decisions under the Canada Labour Code are generally final and not subject to court review, with limited exceptions for judicial review in cases of jurisdictional error or failure to observe administrative fairness.

question: What are the general powers and authorities granted to an arbitrator or arbitration board in the context of labor disputes and collective agreements under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## General Powers and Authorities of Arbitrators and Arbitration Boards

### Section 60(1) - Broadly Defined Powers

Section 60(1) outlines the general powers vested in an arbitrator or arbitration board. It states that they possess:
"(a) the powers conferred on the Board by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c) and (f.1); (a.1) the power to interpret, apply and give relief in accordance with a statute relating to employment matters, whether or not there is conflict between the statute and the collective agreement; (a.2) the power to make the interim orders that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate; (a.3) the power to consider submissions provided in the form that the arbitrator or the arbitration board considers appropriate or to which the parties agree; (a.4) the power to expedite proceedings and to prevent abuse of the arbitration process by making the orders or giving the directions that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate for those purposes; and (b) power to determine any question as to whether a matter referred to the arbitrator or arbitration board is arbitrable."

This section establishes a broad foundation for the arbitrator's authority. The arbitrator's powers are not limited to the scope of the collective agreement itself but also extend to interpreting and applying relevant statutes. This is significant because it allows the arbitrator to consider broader legal principles when resolving disputes.

### Section 60(1)(a.1) - Statutory Interpretation and Relief
"...the power to interpret, apply and give relief in accordance with a statute relating to employment matters, whether or not there is conflict between the statute and the collective agreement..."

This provision is crucial. It grants the arbitrator the power to interpret and apply statutes related to employment matters, even if those statutes conflict with the terms of the collective agreement. This ensures that the arbitration process is not solely bound by the agreement's wording and can consider broader legal obligations.

### Section 60(1)(a.2) - Interim Orders
"...the power to make the interim orders that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate..."

Arbitrators have the authority to issue interim orders. This allows them to take action to maintain the status quo or prevent irreparable harm during the arbitration process. These orders can be crucial in managing disputes effectively.

### Section 60(1)(a.3) - Submission Formats
"...the power to consider submissions provided in the form that the arbitrator or the arbitration board considers appropriate or to which the parties agree..."

This provision gives the arbitrator flexibility in how they receive information. They can dictate the format of submissions to ensure clarity and efficiency, or they can agree on a format with the parties.

### Section 60(1)(a.4) - Expediting Proceedings
"...the power to expedite proceedings and to prevent abuse of the arbitration process by making the orders or giving the directions that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate for those purposes..."

Arbitrators have the power to manage the arbitration process efficiently. They can expedite proceedings and prevent abuse, ensuring that the process is fair and timely.

### Section 60(1)(b) - Determining Arbitrability
"...power to determine any question as to whether a matter referred to the arbitrator or arbitration board is arbitrable."

This power is fundamental. The arbitrator has the authority to decide whether a particular dispute falls within the scope of arbitration. This ensures that only appropriate matters are submitted to the arbitration process.

### Section 60(1.1) - Extending Time
"The arbitrator or arbitration board may extend the time for taking any step in the grievance process or arbitration procedure set out in a collective agreement, even after the expiration of the time, if the arbitrator or arbitration board is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for the extension and that the other party would not be unduly prejudiced by the extension."

Arbitrators have the power to extend timelines within the grievance or arbitration process, provided there are reasonable grounds for the extension and the other party is not unduly prejudiced. This allows for flexibility in resolving complex issues.

### Section 60(1.2) - Assistance in Resolving Differences
"At any stage of a proceeding before an arbitrator or arbitration board, the arbitrator or arbitration board may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving the difference at issue without prejudice to the power of the arbitrator or arbitration board to continue the arbitration with respect to the issues that have not been resolved."

Arbitrators can facilitate settlement discussions between the parties, even if they continue to pursue the arbitration process. This promotes a collaborative approach to dispute resolution.

### Section 60(2) - Substitution of Penalty
"Where an arbitrator or arbitration board determines that an employee has been discharged or disciplined by an employer for cause and the collective agreement does not contain a specific penalty for the infraction that is the subject of the arbitration, the arbitrator or arbitration board has power to substitute for the discharge or discipline such other penalty as to the arbitrator or arbitration board seems just and reasonable in the circumstances."

In cases where the collective agreement lacks a specific penalty for an infraction, the arbitrator has the power to substitute a penalty that is deemed just and reasonable. This allows for flexibility in addressing disciplinary matters.
