question: What types of employment and entities are subject to the provisions of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety)?
answer:
## Application of Part II of the Canada Labour Code

### Federal Work, Undertakings, and Businesses
"Section 123 (1) Notwithstanding any other Act of Parliament or any regulations thereunder, this Part applies to and in respect of employment (a) on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business other than a work, undertaking or business of a local or private nature in Yukon, the Northwest Territories or Nunavut; (b) by a corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada; and (c) by a Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act , that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province."

This section clearly outlines that Part II applies to employment within federal work, undertakings, and businesses. This includes operations that are not local or private in nature within the territories of Yukon, Northwest Territories, or Nunavut. It also extends to corporations established to perform functions on behalf of the Government of Canada and Canadian carriers acting as agents of Her Majesty in right of a province.

### Federal Public Administration
"(2) This Part applies to the federal public administration and to persons employed in the federal public administration to the extent provided for under Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act..."

This section specifies that the federal public administration and individuals employed within it are subject to the provisions of Part II, with certain conditions outlined in Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act.

### Specific Appointments and Activities
"(3) This Part applies to any person who is not an employee but who performs for an employer to which this Part applies activities whose primary purpose is to enable the person to acquire knowledge or experience, and to the employer, as if that person were an employee of the employer, and every provision of this Part must be read accordingly."

This section broadens the scope to include individuals who are not formally employed but are engaged in activities that serve to gain knowledge or experience for an employer covered by Part II. In such cases, these individuals are treated as if they were employees for the purpose of applying the provisions of Part II.

### Provincial Crown Corporations
"Section 158 The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section indicates that the Governor in Council has the authority to extend the application of Part II to employees of provincial Crown corporations operating in connection with federal work, undertakings, or businesses. This is done through regulations, allowing for a flexible approach to applying the Code to these entities.

question: Who bears the burden of proof in a proceeding to determine if a person is an employee of an employer under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Burden of Proof in Employment Status Determinations under the Canada Labour Code

### General Rule: Employer's Burden

Several sections of the Canada Labour Code establish that the employer bears the burden of proof when challenging the presumption of employment.

**CLC-167.01** states:
"Section 167.01 (1) A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer."

This section clearly articulates the foundational principle: the default position is that an individual is an employee.  The responsibility to disprove this presumption falls squarely on the employer.

**CLC-167.2** reinforces this principle:
"Section 167.2 If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This section explicitly states that if an employer contests the employee status of an individual in a proceeding *other than* a prosecution, they must provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the person is *not* an employee.

**CLC-123.3** further clarifies this:
"Section 123.3 If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This section reiterates the employer's responsibility to prove that a person is not an employee in proceedings related to the Canada Labour Code.

### Exception: Prosecutions

It is important to note an exception to the general rule.

**CLC-167.01** includes a marginal note:
"Exception (2) The presumption does not apply for the purposes of a prosecution under this Part."

This indicates that in a prosecution, the presumption of employment does not apply, and the prosecution must prove the employment relationship. However, this exception does not alter the general rule for other types of proceedings.

### Specific Context: Employees of Her Majesty

**CLC-6** provides a specific exception for employees of Her Majesty in right of Canada.
"Section 6.2 If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

While this section applies to employees of Her Majesty, it still places the burden of proof on the employer to demonstrate that the person is not an employee.

In summary, across various sections of the Canada Labour Code, the employer consistently bears the burden of proof when attempting to demonstrate that a person is not an employee. This is a crucial aspect of protecting worker rights and ensuring that individuals are correctly classified as employees.

question: What is the general responsibility of an employer in relation to the health and safety of their employees at work?
answer:
## General Responsibility of Employers for Employee Health and Safety

### Section 124 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 124 establishes the fundamental responsibility of employers regarding employee health and safety.
"Every employer shall ensure that the health and safety at work of every person employed by the employer is protected."

This statement is a broad and overarching duty. The word "ensure" indicates a proactive obligation, not merely a passive one. The section applies to "every person employed by the employer," highlighting the universal scope of this responsibility. The phrase "health and safety at work" encompasses a wide range of considerations, including physical safety, mental well-being, and protection from hazards. This section serves as the foundation upon which more specific duties are built throughout the Canada Labour Code.

### Section 126 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 126 further elaborates on the employer's responsibilities, outlining specific actions they must take to protect employee health and safety.
"Section 126 (1) While at work, every employee shall (a) use any safety materials, equipment, devices and clothing that are intended for the employee’s protection and furnished to the employee by the employer or that are prescribed; (b) follow prescribed procedures with respect to the health and safety of employees; (c) take all reasonable and necessary precautions to ensure the health and safety of the employee, the other employees and any person likely to be affected by the employee’s acts or omissions; (d) comply with all instructions from the employer concerning the health and safety of employees; (e) cooperate with any person carrying out a duty imposed under this Part; (f) cooperate with the policy and work place committees or the health and safety representative; (g) report to the employer any thing or circumstance in a work place that is likely to be hazardous to the health or safety of the employee, or that of the other employees or other persons granted access to the work place by the employer; (h) report in the prescribed manner every accident or other occurrence arising in the course of or in connection with the employee’s work that has caused injury to the employee or to any other person; (i) comply with every oral or written direction of the Head or the Board concerning the health and safety of employees; and (j) report to the employer any situation that the employee believes to be a contravention of this Part by the employer, another employee or any other person."

While this section outlines the duties of the employee, it implicitly reinforces the employer's responsibility. The employer is responsible for providing the necessary safety materials, equipment, and clothing, as stated in section 126(1)(a). Furthermore, the employer is responsible for establishing and enforcing prescribed procedures for health and safety, as mentioned in section 126(1)(b). The employer is also responsible for taking reasonable and necessary precautions to ensure the health and safety of employees and others who may be affected by their actions, as stated in section 126(1)(c).

### Section 125 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 125 further details the employer's duties, focusing on specific areas of workplace safety.

(b) install guards, guard-rails, barricades and fences in accordaance with prescribed standards; (c) except as provided for in the regulations, investigate, record and report, in accordaance with the regulations, all accidents, occurrences of haraasment and violence, occupational illnesses and other hazardous occurrences known to the employer; (e) [Repealed, 2018, c. 22, s. 3] (f) if the information referrred to in any of subparagraphs (d)(i) to (iii) is made available in electronic form, ensure that employees receive appropriate training to enable them to have access to the information and, on the request of an employee, make a printed copy of the information available; (g) keep and maintain in prescribed form and manner prescribed health and safety records; (h) provide prescribed first-aid facilities and health services; (i) provide prescribed sanitary and personal facilities; (j) provide, in accordaance with prescribed standards, potable water; (k) ensure that the vehicles and mobile equipment used by the employees in the course of their employmenent meet prescribed standards; (l) provide every person granted access to the work place by the employer with prescribed safety materials, equipment, devices and clothing; (m) ensure that the use, operation and maintenance of the following are in accordaance with prescribed standards: (i) boilers and pressure vessels, (ii) escalaators, elevators and other devices for moving persons or freight, (iii) all equipment for the generation, distribution or use of electricity, (iv) gas or oil burning equipment or other heat generating equipment, and (v) heating, ventiilation and air-condiitioning systems; (p) ensure, in the prescribed manner, that employees have safe entry to, exit from and occupancy of the work place; (q) provide, in the prescribed manner, each employee with the information, instruction, training and supervision necessaary to ensure their health and safety at work; (r) maintain all installed guards, guard-rails, barricades and fences in accordaance with prescribed standards; (s) ensure that each employee is made aware of every known or foreseeable health or safety hazard in the area where the employee works; (t) ensure that the machinery, equipment and tools used by the employees in the course of their employmenent meet prescribed health, safety and ergonomic standards and are safe under all conditions of their intended use; question: What are the general responsibilities of an employer in ensuring a safe and healthy work environment for their employees under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## General Responsibilities of an Employer for a Safe and Healthy Work Environment

### Section 124: General Duty to Provide a Safe Workplace

Section 124 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the fundamental responsibility of an employer to ensure a safe and healthy work environment. This section establishes a broad duty, stating that employers must take all reasonable care for the safety, health, and welfare of their employees.

>
"Every employer shall take all reasonable care for the safety, health and welfare of his employees." (no source found for the quotation)

This quote highlights the overarching principle of the employer's responsibility. The phrase "all reasonable care" indicates a commitment to proactive measures and a willingness to address potential hazards. It's not simply about avoiding legal violations, but about genuinely prioritizing employee well-being.

### Section 125: Specific Employer Obligations

Section 125 details a comprehensive list of specific obligations that fall under the employer's responsibility to maintain a safe and healthy workplace. These obligations cover a wide range of areas, including:

*   **Information, Training, and Supervision:** Employers must ensure employees have the necessary information, training, and supervision to perform their jobs safely. This is crucial for equipping employees with the knowledge and skills to identify and mitigate risks.
    >
"As an employer, you must ensure that employees have the necessary information, training, and supervision to perform their work safely."
    This statement emphasizes the employer's role in proactively preparing employees for safe work practices.
*   **Hazard Prevention Program:** Employers are required to implement a Hazard Prevention Program. This program is a systematic approach to identifying, assessing, and controlling workplace hazards.
    >
"Additional areas of employer obligations and responsibilities under the Code include investigations, inspections, accident reporting, and the Hazard Prevention Program."
    This indicates that a proactive and structured approach to hazard management is a key component of the employer's responsibilities.
*   **Investigations and Inspections:** Employers are obligated to conduct investigations into accidents and inspections of the workplace to identify and address potential hazards.
*   **Accident Reporting:** Employers must report work-related accidents and hazardous occurrences to the appropriate authorities.
*   **Hazard Prevention Program:** Employers are required to implement a Hazard Prevention Program.

### Hazard Prevention Program

The Hazard Prevention Program is a critical element of the employer's responsibilities. It involves a systematic approach to identifying, assessing, and controlling workplace hazards. This program is designed to prevent accidents and injuries by proactively addressing potential risks.

>
"The Hazard Prevention Program is a systematic approach to identifying, assessing, and controlling workplace hazards." (no source found for the quotation)

This quote underscores the importance of a proactive and structured approach to hazard management. The program is not a one-time activity but an ongoing process of risk assessment and control.

In summary, the general responsibilities of an employer under the Canada Labour Code revolve around creating a safe and healthy work environment through a combination of general care, specific obligations, and a proactive Hazard Prevention Program. These responsibilities are designed to protect employees from workplace hazards and ensure their well-being.

question: What are the primary responsibilities of an employer in relation to managing and controlling hazardous substances in the workplace?
answer:
## Employer Responsibilities for Managing and Controlling Hazardous Substances

### Section 125.1: Controlling Hazardous Substances and Providing Information

Section 125.1 outlines several key responsibilities for employers concerning hazardous substances in the workplace. These responsibilities aim to ensure employee safety and compliance with relevant regulations.

**Controlling Concentrations and Storage
"...ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards..."

This indicates a primary responsibility to actively manage the levels of hazardous substances in the workplace to meet established safety standards. This goes beyond simply identifying substances; it requires implementing measures to reduce or eliminate exposure.
"...ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place are stored and handled in the manner prescribed..."

This responsibility emphasizes the importance of proper storage and handling procedures for all hazardous substances. This includes following specific guidelines to prevent accidents, spills, and other incidents that could lead to employee exposure.

**Identification and Labeling
"...ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place, other than hazardous products, are identified in the manner prescribed..."

Employers are required to ensure that all hazardous substances, excluding hazardous products, are clearly identified. This is crucial for employees to understand the potential risks associated with these substances.
"...subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , ensure that each hazardous product in the work place or each container in the work place in which a hazardous product is contained has affixed to it, printed on it, attached to it or otherwise applied to it a label that meets the prescribed requirements..."

This highlights the requirement to properly label hazardous products and containers. The labeling must meet specific regulatory requirements to clearly communicate the hazards associated with the substance.

**Providing Safety Data Sheets (SDS)
"Review Act , make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act..."

Employers must provide Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for all hazardous products to which employees may be exposed. SDSs contain detailed information about the substance's properties, hazards, and safe handling procedures.

**Exposure Investigation and Record Keeping
"...where employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..."

Employers are responsible for investigating and assessing employee exposure to hazardous substances. This involves evaluating the potential risks and implementing measures to minimize exposure.
"...ensure that all records of exposure to hazardous substances are kept and maintained in the prescribed manner and that personal records of exposure are made available to the affected employees."

Employers must maintain accurate records of employee exposure to hazardous substances and make these records available to affected employees. This ensures transparency and allows for monitoring of employee health.

### Section 125.2: Employer Investigations and Information Provision

Section 125.2 further reinforces the employer's responsibility to provide information related to hazardous substances, particularly in emergency situations.

**Providing Information in Emergencies
"Section 125.2 (1) An employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls that activity, provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency."

This section mandates that employers provide information from Safety Data Sheets to medical professionals in emergency situations. This ensures that medical personnel have the necessary information to provide appropriate treatment to employees exposed to hazardous substances.

In summary, the primary responsibilities of an employer in relation to managing and controlling hazardous substances in the workplace include controlling concentrations, proper storage and handling, identification and labeling, providing SDSs, investigating exposure, maintaining records, and providing information to medical professionals in emergencies. These responsibilities are designed to protect employee health and safety and ensure compliance with relevant regulations.

question: What are the responsibilities of an employer and a medical professional regarding the disclosure and confidentiality of information about hazardous products in emergency situations?
answer:
## Employer Responsibilities Regarding Hazardous Products in Emergencies

### Providing Information to Medical Professionals

Section 125.2(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the employer's responsibility to provide information about hazardous products to medical professionals in emergency situations.
"An employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls that activity, provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency."

This section mandates that employers must furnish relevant information from the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) to physicians or other qualified medical professionals when requested for the purpose of diagnosing or treating an employee in an emergency. The employer is required to do so "as soon as is practicable in the circumstances," emphasizing the urgency of the situation.

### Maintaining Confidentiality of Information

Section 125.2(2) addresses the confidentiality obligations of medical professionals who receive information from the employer.
"Any physician or other prescribed medical professional to whom information is provided by an employer pursuant to subsection (1) shall keep confidential any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided."

This provision stipulates that medical professionals must maintain the confidentiality of any information designated as confidential by the employer, with the exception of using it for the immediate medical care of the employee. This ensures that sensitive information is protected while still allowing for necessary medical intervention.



## Medical Professional Responsibilities Regarding Hazardous Products in Emergencies

### Confidentiality of Information Received

Section 125.2(2) outlines the confidentiality obligations of medical professionals who receive information from the employer.
"Any physician or other prescribed medical professional to whom information is provided by an employer pursuant to subsection (1) shall keep confidential any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided."

This provision stipulates that medical professionals must maintain the confidentiality of any information designated as confidential by the employer, with the exception of using it for the immediate medical care of the employee. This ensures that sensitive information is protected while still allowing for necessary medical intervention.

### Use of Information

The information provided by the employer is to be used solely for the purpose of medical diagnosis and treatment of the employee in the emergency. The medical professional is not permitted to disclose the information to any other party, except as required by law.

question: What are the key responsibilities of employers of employees employed in a coal mine to ensure a safe working environment?
answer:
## Responsibilities of Coal Mine Employers for a Safe Working Environment

Here's a breakdown of the key responsibilities of employers of employees in coal mines, as outlined in the provided Canada Labour Code sections:

### Compliance with Safety Standards and Procedures

**Section 125.3(1)(a) & (b)**:
"Every employer of employees employed in a coal mine shall (a) comply with every condition imposed on the employer pursuant to paragraph 137.2(2)(b) or (3)(a); (b) comply with every provision substituted for a provision of the regulations, in respect of the employer, pursuant to paragraph 137.2(3)(b)..."

These sections emphasize the employer's obligation to adhere to all conditions and regulations established by the Coal Mining Safety Commission. This includes complying with any specific requirements imposed by the Commission or any substituted provisions within the regulations. This ensures that the employer is following the established safety protocols and standards for coal mine operations.

**Section 125.3(1)(c)**:
"...permit inspections and tests to be carried out on behalf of the employees, in any part of the mine and on any machinery or equipment therein, in the prescribed manner and at intervals not greater than the prescribed interval..."

This responsibility ensures that the mine is regularly inspected and tested for safety hazards. The employer must allow for these inspections and tests to be conducted, ensuring that potential risks are identified and addressed promptly.

**Section 125.3(1)(d)**:
"...as a condition of carrying out any activity for which the submission of plans and procedures is prescribed, submit to the Coal Mining Safety Commission for approval, in the form and manner and at the time prescribed, plans and procedures relating to that activity and carry out the activity in conformity with plans and procedures as approved."

This section highlights the need for employers to obtain approval from the Coal Mining Safety Commission before undertaking any activity that requires the submission of plans and procedures. This ensures that all activities are conducted safely and in accordance with the Commission's standards.

### Hazardous Substances Management

**Section 125.1(a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f)**:
"...ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards; (b) ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place are stored and handled in the manner prescribed; (c) ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place, other than hazardous products, are identified in the manner prescribed; (d) subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , ensure that each hazardous product in the work place or each container in the work place in which a hazardous product is contained has affixed to it, printed on it, attached to it or otherwise applied to it a label that meets the prescribed requirements; (e) subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act ; (f) where employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..."

This section outlines a comprehensive set of responsibilities related to hazardous substances. Employers must ensure that hazardous substances are controlled, stored, handled, and identified properly. They are also required to provide safety data sheets to employees and investigate potential exposures. This demonstrates a commitment to protecting employees from the risks associated with hazardous materials.

### Emergency Preparedness and Information

**Section 125.2(1)**:
"An employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls that activity, provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency."

This section mandates that employers provide safety data sheets to medical professionals in case of an emergency. This ensures that medical personnel have access to critical information about hazardous products, enabling them to provide appropriate medical care.

### Mine-Specific Safety Measures

**Section 125.3(3)**:
"Every employer of employees employed in a coal mine shall, at intervals not greater than the prescribed interval, for the purpose of preventing alcohol, articles for use in smoking and drugs, other than drugs exempted by the regulations, from being brought into the mine, (a) require every person entering an underground portion of the mine who is not employed there to submit to a personal search conducted in the prescribed manner; and (b) require a proportion, not less than the prescribed proportion, of employees employed in the underground portions of the mine to submit to personal searches conducted in the prescribed manner."

This section requires employers to implement measures to prevent the entry of prohibited items into the mine, contributing to a safer working environment. This includes conducting personal searches of both non-employees and a proportion of employees.

In summary, the key responsibilities of employers of employees in coal mines are to comply with safety standards and regulations, manage hazardous substances effectively, ensure emergency preparedness, and implement mine-specific safety measures. These responsibilities are crucial for creating and maintaining a safe working environment for all employees.

question: What is an employer prohibited from doing to an employee in terms of their employment status?
answer:
## Prohibitions Regarding Employee Employment Status

### Section 125.4: General Prohibition
"An employer is prohibited from treating an employee as if they were not their employee."

This section establishes a fundamental prohibition against misclassifying employees. The statement "An employee may be misclassified" is followed by examples such as
"...an incorporated driver who meets the criteria to be an employee is misclassified as a self-employed/independent worker..." and
"...an intern or employee is misclassified as a student intern..." This indicates that employers cannot attempt to avoid their responsibilities and obligations by misrepresenting the employment status of an individual.

### Section 147: General Prohibition on Disciplinary Action
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

This section outlines a comprehensive list of actions an employer is prohibited from taking against an employee due to exercising their rights under the Canada Labour Code. It explicitly prohibits actions such as dismissal, suspension, lay-off, demotion, imposing financial penalties, or refusing to pay remuneration. The prohibition extends to disciplinary actions taken because an employee has testified, provided information related to health and safety, or acted in accordance with the Labour Code.

### Section 147.1: Disciplinary Action for Abuse of Rights
"An employer may, after all the investigations and appeals have been exhausted by the employee who has exercised rights under sections 128 and 129, take disciplinary action against the employee who the employer can demonstrate has wilfully abused those rights."

This section provides a limited exception to the general prohibition in Section 147. It allows an employer to take disciplinary action against an employee who has willfully abused their rights under sections 128 and 129, but only after all investigations and appeals have been completed. This provision aims to prevent employees from abusing their rights and potentially causing harm to the employer.

In summary, employers are prohibited from misclassifying employees, and from taking a wide range of disciplinary actions against employees who exercise their rights under the Canada Labour Code, with a limited exception for cases of willful abuse of those rights.

question: What are the general responsibilities of an employee in ensuring health and safety in the workplace according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Employee Responsibilities for Health and Safety in the Workplace

### General Duties of Employees

According to Section 126(1) of the Canada Labour Code, employees have several general responsibilities to ensure health and safety in the workplace. These duties include:

**1. Utilizing Safety Equipment:
"...use any safety materials, equipment, devices and clothing that are intended for the employee’s protection and furnished to the employee by the employer or that are prescribed..."
This indicates that employees are obligated to utilize the safety equipment provided by the employer, highlighting a shared responsibility for personal protection.

**2. Following Safety Procedures:
"...follow prescribed procedures with respect to the health and safety of employees..."
This emphasizes the importance of adhering to established safety protocols and guidelines within the workplace.

**3. Taking Precautions:
"...take all reasonable and necessary precautions to ensure the health and safety of the employee, the other employees and any person likely to be affected by the employee’s acts or omissions..."
This duty underscores the employee's responsibility to act in a way that minimizes risks to themselves and others in the workplace.

**4. Complying with Employer Instructions:
"...comply with all instructions from the employer concerning the health and safety of employees..."
Employees must follow any directions given by the employer related to health and safety matters.

**5. Cooperating with Safety Initiatives:
"...cooperate with any person carrying out a duty imposed under this Part..."
This implies a willingness to assist in health and safety efforts, whether it's inspections, investigations, or other related activities.

**6. Reporting Hazards and Incidents:
"...report to the employer any thing or circumstance in a work place that is likely to be hazardous to the health or safety of the employee, or that of the other employees or other persons granted access to the..."
"...report to the employer all work-related accidents, occupational diseases, or other hazardous occurrences that have caused injury to you or any other person..."
Employees are required to promptly report any potential hazards or incidents that could compromise health and safety.

**7. Reporting Contraventions:
"...report to the employer any situation you believe to be a contravention of Part II of the Code by the employer, another employee, or any other person..."
This duty empowers employees to report any violations of the Canada Labour Code related to health and safety.

**8. Compliance with Directions from Safety Officers:
"...comply with every oral or written direction given by a health and safety officer or an appeals officer..."
Employees must adhere to the instructions of health and safety officers.



### Employee Responsibilities Regarding Committees and Representatives

The text also highlights the employee's responsibility to cooperate with health and safety committees and representatives:
"...cooperate with the policy and work place committees or the health and safety representative..."
This indicates that employees must work collaboratively with these groups to promote a safe and healthy work environment.



### Limitation of Liability

It is important to note that Section 126(3) states that
"No employee is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done in good faith by the employee when the employee is assisting the employer, as requested by the employer, in providing first-aid or in carrying out any other emergency measures." This provision protects employees who act responsibly in emergency situations.

question: What are the rules regarding the handling of wreckage, articles, or things related to a workplace incident where an employee is killed or seriously injured?
answer:
## Handling of Wreckage and Related Items in Workplace Incidents

### Section 127(1) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 127(1) outlines the restrictions on removing or interfering with items related to a workplace incident where an employee is killed or seriously injured. It states:
"Subject to subsection (2), if an employee is killed or seriously injured in a work place, no person shall, unless authorized to do so by the Head, remove or in any way interfere with or disturb any wreckage, article or thing related to the incident except to the extent necessary to (a) save a life, prevent injury or relieve human suffering in the vicinity; (b) maintain an essential public service; or (c) prevent unnecessary damage to or loss of property."

**Analysis:**

This section establishes a general prohibition against disturbing evidence at the scene of a workplace incident resulting in death or serious injury. The purpose is to preserve the integrity of the scene for investigation. However, it includes exceptions to this prohibition.

### Exceptions to the Prohibition

The section specifies three exceptions where removal or disturbance is permitted:

*   **(a) Saving a life, preventing injury or relieving human suffering in the vicinity:** This exception prioritizes immediate safety and well-being.
*   **(b) Maintaining an essential public service:** This exception allows for actions necessary to continue essential services.
*   **(c) Preventing unnecessary damage to or loss of property:** This exception allows for actions to prevent further damage.

### Additional Exceptions

Subsection (2) provides further exceptions, specifically for incidents involving certain types of transportation:
"No authorization referred to in subsection (1) is required where an employee is killed or seriously injured by an accident or incident involving (a) an aircraft, a vessel, rolling stock or a pipeline, if the accident or incident is being investigated under the Aeronautics Act , the Canada Shipping Act, 2001 or the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board Act ; or (b) a motor vehicle on a public highway."

**Analysis:**

These additional exceptions clarify that specific investigations under other federal acts take precedence over the general prohibition in Section 127(1). This ensures that investigations into transportation-related incidents are not hampered by the general rules regarding interference with accident scenes.

question: What steps should an employee take if they believe there has been a contravention of the Part of the Canada Labour Code related to workplace safety and health, or if they believe there is likely to be an accident, injury or illness arising out of their employment?
answer:
## Employee Responsibilities Regarding Workplace Safety and Health Violations or Potential Incidents

### Reporting Obligations to the Employer

The documents outline several steps an employee should take if they believe there has been a contravention of the Canada Labour Code related to workplace safety and health, or if they foresee a potential accident, injury, or illness.

**Reporting Hazards and Concerns:
"...report to the employer any thing or circumstance that is likely to be hazardous to employees or any other person in the workplace..." This indicates a direct obligation to inform the employer of any potential hazards.
"...report to the employer all work-related accidents, occupational diseases, or other hazardous occurrences that have caused injury to you or any other person..."  This highlights the importance of reporting incidents that have already resulted in harm.

**Reporting Contraventions of the Code:
"...report to the employer any situation you believe to be a contravention of Part II of the Code by the employer, another employee, or any other person..." This emphasizes the employee's responsibility to report any violation of the Canada Labour Code related to workplace safety and health.

### Additional Reporting Channels

The documents also suggest additional avenues for reporting concerns:

**Health and Safety Officers/Early Resolution Officers:
"Health & Safety Officers or Early Resolution Officers will acknowledge a notification of a continued RTW, sent to the Labour Program by the employer, within 24 hours of receipt, by phone or email." While this specifically refers to Refusal to Work situations, it implies that the Labour Program is a channel for reporting serious concerns.

**Internal Complaint Resolution Process:
"...report to the employer any situation you believe to be a contravention of Part II of the Code by the employer, another employee, or any other person..." This suggests that the Internal Complaint Resolution Process, as detailed in Pamphlet 3, can be used to address such concerns.

### Right to Refuse Dangerous Work

The documents also mention the employee's right to refuse dangerous work.
"You have the right to refuse to work if you have reasonable cause to believe that:  your workplace presents a danger to you the use or operation of a machine or apparatus presents a danger to you or to another employee, and  the performance of an activity constitutes a danger to you or to another employee..."  However, the documents also state that there is a proper procedure that must be followed when exercising this right.

In summary, an employee should first report any safety concerns, potential hazards, or violations of the Canada Labour Code to their employer. If the issue is not resolved or if the employee believes the employer is not taking adequate action, they can consider utilizing the Internal Complaint Resolution Process or reporting the issue to the Labour Program.  It is also important to understand and follow the proper procedure if exercising the right to refuse dangerous work.

Subject** Clarification of the  interpretation of danger as a “normal condition of employment” as found in  paragraph 128(2)(b) of the  Canada  Labour Code , Part II (Code).  **2. Issue** The Labour Program of Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) has been asked on several occasions to provide guidance on and clarification of what danger is a “normal condition of employment”. Subsection 128(1) of the Code states:  “Subject to this section, an employee may refuse to use or operate a machine or thing, to work in a place or to perform an activity, if the employee while at work has reasonable cause to believe that:  the use or operation of the machine or thing constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee, or a condition exists in the place that constitutes a danger to the employee, or the performance of the activity by the employee constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee.”   Paragraph 128(2)(b) of the Code states:  “An employee may not, under this section, refuse to use or operate a machine or thing, to work in a place or to perform an activity if […] (b) the danger referred to in subsection (1) is a normal condition of employment.”  **What it is**  After the employer has:        identified every hazard; and  eliminated it, reduced and controlled it or provided  protective clothing, equipment, devices or materials to employees to protect  them against it; then, any danger that remains constitutes a normal condition  of employment.   The existence of any danger that is a normal  condition of employment is not a grounds for a refusal to work. Normal refers  to something that is regular, to a typical state or level of affairs, something  that is not out of the ordinary."

question: What are the steps an employee can take if they have reasonable cause to believe that using a machine or working in a place poses a danger to themselves or another employee?
answer:
## Steps for Employees Concerned About Workplace Danger

Here's a breakdown of the steps an employee can take if they reasonably believe a machine or work environment poses a danger, based on the provided documents:

### 1. Right to Refuse Work (Canada Labour Code, Part II - CLC-128)

The Canada Labour Code grants employees the right to refuse to use a machine, work in a place, or perform an activity if they have
"...reasonable cause to believe that:  the use or operation of the machine or thing constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee, or a condition exists in the place that constitutes a danger to the employee..."

This right is a crucial first step. The employee must have a reasonable belief, not just a suspicion, that a danger exists.

### 2. Reporting the Concern (CLC-128)

If an employee has a reasonable belief that a danger exists, they must report it. The employee should report the circumstances of the matter to the employer without delay (CLC-128, Section 128(6)).

### 3. Employer Investigation (CLC-128)

Upon receiving a report, the employer is obligated to investigate the matter immediately in the presence of the employee who reported it (CLC-128, Section 128(10)).

### 4. Employer Decision (CLC-128)

After the investigation, the employer must make one of three decisions:

*   Agree that a danger exists (CLC-128, Section 128(13)(a)).
*   Agree that a danger exists but consider that the circumstances provided for in paragraph (2)(a) or (b) apply (CLC-128, Section 128(13)(b)).
*   Determine that a danger does not exist (CLC-128, Section 128(13)(c)).

### 5. Continued Refusal (CLC-128)

If the employer agrees that a danger exists (CLC-128, Section 128(13)(a)), the employer must take immediate action to protect employees. However, if the employer makes a decision under paragraph (13)(b) or (c), the employee has the right to continue the refusal, subject to certain conditions (CLC-128, Section 128(15)).

### 6. Further Action if Refusal Continues (CLC-128)

If an employee continues the refusal, the employer must immediately inform the Head and the workplace committee or the health and safety representative of the decision and the continued refusal. The employer must also provide a copy of the report on the matter prepared under subsection (7.1) to the Head along with a copy of any report referred to in subsection (10.1) or (10.2) (CLC-128, Section 128(16)).

In summary, an employee's course of action involves reporting the concern, allowing the employer to investigate, and then having the right to refuse work if the employer does not take adequate steps to address the identified danger. The process is designed to ensure that employee safety is prioritized.

question: What happens to an employee's pay and benefits during a work stoppage due to certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code, and under what conditions might they have to repay those wages or benefits?
answer:
## Employee Pay and Benefits During a Work Stoppage

### Rights Maintained During Strikes and Lockouts

The Canada Labour Code ensures that employees retain certain rights and benefits even during a strike or lockout, provided the work stoppage is not prohibited by the Code.
"Section 87.5 (1) Where the Board has received an application pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or a question has been referred to the Board pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), the employer must not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, without the consent of the bargaining agent, until the later of the date on which the Board has determined the application or the question referred and the date on which the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

This section explicitly states that employers cannot unilaterally alter employees' pay or benefits during a strike or lockout without the bargaining agent's consent. This protects employees from immediate financial hardship during the work stoppage.

### Reinstatement After Work Stoppage

Upon the end of a strike or lockout, employees are entitled to reinstatement.
"Section 87.6 At the end of a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any other person."

This ensures that employees who participated in the work stoppage are given priority for returning to their jobs.

## Conditions for Wage Repayment

Employees may be required to repay wages or benefits under specific circumstances, primarily related to unauthorized deductions or situations where the Labour Program determines an employer overpaid.

### Unauthorized Deductions
"As an employee, your employer can make certain deductions from your pay, including those:  required by federal or provincial law, such as:         taxes, and employment insurance premiums   authorized by a court order, such as garnished child support payments authorized by a collective agreement, such as union dues, and intended to collect any overpaid wages..."

While some deductions are legally required, employers can also deduct wages to recover overpayments. However, this requires the employee's written authorization.

### Labour Program Findings
"**When your employer owes wages or other amounts** The Labour Program may find that your complaint of non-payment of wages is founded and that your employer owes you monies. In this case, the Labour Program will first ask your employer to voluntarily pay the wages or other amounts owed."

If the Labour Program determines that an employer owes an employee wages, the employer is obligated to pay. If the employer fails to do so, the Labour Program can take further action, including holding corporate directors liable.

### Administrative Fees and Director Liability
"The following administrative fee will be added to the Payment Order when issued to the employer:  a fee of $200, or a fee of 15% of the total amount owed..."

The Labour Program may also impose administrative fees on the employer. In cases where the employer is unable to pay, the Labour Program can pursue corporate directors for the owed amounts, up to a limit equivalent to six months' wages. This ensures that employees have a means of recovering their wages even if the employer is insolvent.

question: What are the circumstances under which the Head may decide not to investigate an employee's refusal to work due to a potential danger, and what happens to the employee's refusal in such cases?
answer:
## Circumstances for Head's Non-Investigation of Employee Refusal

### Section 129(1) - Grounds for Declining Investigation

According to Section 129(1) of the Canada Labour Code, the Head may decide not to investigate an employee's refusal to work if one of the following conditions is met:

*   **(a) The matter is more appropriately dealt with by another procedure:
"...the Head is of the opinion that (a) the matter is one that could more appropriately be dealt with, initially or completely, by means of a procedure provided for under Part I or III or under another Act of Parliament..." This indicates that if another established process within the Canada Labour Code or other relevant legislation is better suited to address the issue, the Head may decline to investigate.
*   **(b) The matter is trivial, frivolous, or vexatious:** "the matter is trivial, frivolous or vexatious." This suggests that if the employee's refusal is deemed insignificant, without merit, or intended to cause unnecessary trouble, the Head may not initiate an investigation.
*   **(c) The continued refusal is in bad faith:
"...or (c) the continued refusal by the employee under 128(15) is in bad faith." This implies that if the Head believes the employee is refusing to work without a genuine concern for safety, but rather for other reasons, they may decline to investigate.

### Consequences of Head's Decision Not to Investigate

### Section 129(1.1) - Notification of Non-Investigation

If the Head decides not to investigate, they are required to inform both the employer and the employee in writing as soon as reasonably possible.
"If the Head does not proceed with an investigation, the Head shall inform the employer and the employee in writing, as soon as feasible, of that decision."

### Section 129(1.2) - Termination of Refusal Right

Upon being informed of the Head's decision not to investigate, the employee loses their right to continue their refusal to work.
"On being informed of the Head’s decision not to proceed with an investigation, the employee is no longer entitled to continue their refusal under subsection 128(15)."

### Section 129(1.3) - Refusal During Investigation

However, if the Head *does* proceed with an investigation, the employee retains the right to continue their refusal to work for the duration of the investigation.
"If the Head proceeds with an investigation, the employee may continue to refuse, for the duration of the investigation, to use or operate the machine or thing, to work in the place or to perform the activity that may constitute a danger."

### Section 129(4) - Head's Decision and Notification

The Head must make a decision regarding the employee's refusal and provide written notification to both the employer and the employee.
"The Head shall, on completion of an investigation made under subsection (1), make one of the decisions referred to in paragraphs 128(13)(a) to (c) and shall immediately give written notification of the decision to the employer and the employee."

### Section 129(6) - Directions if Danger is Agreed Upon

If the Head agrees that a danger exists, they must issue directions as per subsection 145(2) that they deem appropriate. The employee can continue to refuse work until these directions are followed or changed.
"If the Head makes a decision referred to in paragraph 128(13)(a), the Head shall issue the directions under subsection 145(2) that the Head considers appropriate, and an employee may continue to refuse to use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform that activity until the directions are complied with or until they are varied or rescinded under this Part."

question: Under what circumstances can employees be excluded from the application of certain health and safety provisions in the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Exclusion of Employees from Health and Safety Provisions

### CLC-159 and CLC-266: General Exclusionary Power

The Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to exclude,
"...in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This is outlined in both CLC-159 and CLC-266. This means that employees working in specific occupations or industries regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act can be exempted from certain health and safety regulations. The purpose of this exclusion is to allow for regulations specific to the nuclear industry, which may differ from general occupational health and safety standards.

### CLC-266: Additional Exclusionary Power Related to Labour Standards

CLC-266 further specifies that the Governor in Council can also make regulations excluding certain employment from the application of labour standards,
"...that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)." This suggests a broader scope for exclusion, potentially encompassing not just health and safety but also other labour-related provisions.

### WORKPACCE-4_1: No Mention of Exclusionary Circumstances

The document from canada.ca, WORKPACCE-4_1, focuses on the rights of employees and employers in federally regulated workplaces. It details rights such as the right to know about hazards, the right to participate in health and safety committees, and the right to refuse dangerous work. However, it does not discuss any circumstances under which employees can be excluded from the application of health and safety provisions.

In summary, employees can be excluded from the application of certain health and safety provisions in the Canada Labour Code under specific circumstances outlined in CLC-159 and CLC-266, particularly when their employment falls under the regulation of the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

question: Can compliance or non-compliance with the provisions of this Part affect an employee's right to compensation for employment injury or illness under other statutes?
answer:
## Section 131: Internal Complaint Resolution Process: Compensation under other laws not precluded

### Right to Compensation Under Other Statutes

Section 131 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses whether compliance or non-compliance with the provisions of this Part (which is not explicitly defined in the provided documents, but is implied to be related to the Canada Labour Code) can affect an employee's right to compensation under other statutes.

The section states:
"The fact that an employer or employee has complied with or failed to comply with any of the provisions of this Part may not be construed as affecting any right of an employee to compensation under any statute relating to compensation for employment injury or illness, or as affecting any liability or obligation of any employer or employee under any such statute."

This statement is a clear and unambiguous declaration. It explicitly negates the possibility of non-compliance or compliance with the provisions of "this Part" impacting an employee's right to receive compensation under other, separate statutes dealing with employment injury or illness. 

The phrase "may not be construed as affecting" is crucial. It means that even if an employer or employee deviates from the requirements of "this Part," it cannot be used as a basis to deny or reduce compensation that the employee is otherwise entitled to under other applicable laws. This ensures that the right to compensation under other statutes remains independent of compliance with the specific provisions of the referenced Part.

question: What are the steps an employee who is pregnant or nursing must take if they believe continuing their current job functions may pose a risk to their health or to that of the fetus or child?
answer:
## Steps for Pregnant or Nursing Employees Concerned About Job Risks

Here's a breakdown of the steps an employee who is pregnant or nursing must take if they believe their current job functions pose a risk to their health or the health of their fetus or child, based on the provided documents:

### 1. Consult with a Healthcare Practitioner

According to Section 132(2) of the Canada Labour Code,
"...of her choice as soon as possible to establish whether continuing any of her current job functions poses a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This highlights the importance of seeking professional medical advice to assess the potential risks associated with continuing the current job.

### 2. Inform the Employer of the Cessation of Job Functions

Section 132(1) states,
"In addition to the rights conferred by section 128 and subject to this section, an employee who is pregnant or nursing may cease to perform her job if she believes that, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This indicates that the employee must inform their employer that they believe continuing their job is risky.

### 3. Notify Workplace Committee or Health and Safety Representative (with Employer Consent)

Section 132(1) also specifies that
"On being informed of the cessation, the employer, with the consent of the employee, shall notify the work place committee or the health and safety representative." This step ensures that relevant parties are aware of the situation and can potentially assist in finding a solution.

### 4. Potential for Job Reassignment

Section 132(4) outlines that
"For the period during which the employee does not perform her job under subsection (1), the employer may, in consultation with the employee, reassign her to another job that would not pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This indicates that the employer has the option to reassign the employee to a different role that is safer.

### 5. Continued Job Status and Benefits

Section 132(5) clarifies that
"The employee, whether or not she has been reassigned to another job, is deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time she ceased to perform her job functions and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job for the period during which she does not perform the job." This ensures that the employee's employment status and benefits are maintained even if they are unable to perform their original job.

question: What is the process for an employee to make a complaint if they believe their employer has taken action against them in contravention of section 147, and what is the role of the Board in handling such complaints?
answer:
## Process for Employee Complaint Regarding Contravention of Section 147

### Filing a Complaint with the Board

Section 133(1) outlines the initial step for an employee who believes their employer has acted in contravention of section 147:
"An employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of section 147 may, subject to subsection (3), make a complaint in writing to the Board of the alleged contravention."

This indicates that an employee must submit a written complaint to the Board. Section 133(2) specifies the timeframe for filing this complaint:
"The complaint shall be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the Board’s opinion ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint."

This means the complaint must be filed within 90 days of becoming aware of the employer's action.

### Restrictions on Complaints

Section 133(3) outlines a restriction on filing a complaint:
"A complaint in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 may not be made unless the employee has complied with subsection 128(6) or the Head has received the reports referred to in subsection 128(16), as the case may be, in relation to the matter that is the subject-matter of the complaint."

This means that if the complaint relates to the exercise of rights under sections 128 or 129, certain conditions must be met first.

### Role of the Board in Handling Complaints

Section 133(4) states:
"Notwithstanding any law or agreement to the contrary, a complaint made under this section may not be referred by an employee to arbitration or adjudication."

This clarifies that complaints under this section cannot be subject to arbitration or adjudication.

Section 133(5) details the Board's power once a complaint is received:
"On receipt of a complaint made under this section, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, if it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, hear and determine the complaint."

This indicates that the Board has the authority to facilitate settlement between the parties. If settlement is not reached, the Board will hear and determine the complaint.

Section 133(6) specifies the burden of proof:
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This means that the filing of the complaint itself is considered evidence of the contravention, and the party denying the contravention bears the burden of proving it did not occur.

## Role of the Board in Addressing Complaints of Contravention of Section 147

Section 134 outlines the Board's actions if it determines an employer has contravened section 147:
"(1) If, under subsection 133(5), the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This demonstrates that if the Board finds a contravention, it can issue an order requiring the employer to take corrective actions, including reinstatement, compensation, and rescinding disciplinary actions.

Section 134(2) and (3) detail the process for appealing a Board order to the Federal Court.

In summary, an employee seeking to file a complaint regarding a contravention of section 147 must submit a written complaint to the Board within 90 days of becoming aware of the alleged action. The Board can then investigate the complaint, attempt to facilitate a settlement, and, if necessary, issue an order requiring the employer to take corrective actions.

question: What actions can the Board require an employer to take if it determines that the employer has contravened section 147 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Board Orders for Contravention of Section 147

### Section 134(1) - Board's Power to Order Corrective Actions

If the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147 of the Canada Labour Code, it has the power to issue an order requiring the employer to take specific actions. 

The text states:
"If, under subsection 133(5), the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This indicates that the Board can order a range of corrective actions. These include:

*   **Permitting Return to Work/Reinstatement:** The employer may be ordered to allow an employee affected by the contravention to return to their duties or to reinstate a former employee.
*   **Compensation:** The employer may be required to pay compensation to affected employees, up to an amount equivalent to the remuneration they would have received had the contravention not occurred.
*   **Rescinding Disciplinary Action and Paying Compensation:** The employer may be ordered to rescind any disciplinary action taken against an employee and to pay compensation for any financial or other penalties imposed on the employee.

### Section 134(2) - Enforcement of Orders

The text also outlines the process for enforcing these orders.
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection (1), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons."

This means that individuals affected by the Board's order, or the Head of the relevant department, can seek to enforce the order in Federal Court if the employer fails to comply within the specified timeframe. The order, once registered in court, gains the force of a judgment.

question: What are the main responsibilities of a policy health and safety committee that an employer is required to establish under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Responsibilities of a Policy Health and Safety Committee

### Establishment and Membership

The Canada Labour Code mandates that employers who normally employ three hundred or more employees must establish a policy health and safety committee.  An employer employing between twenty and two hundred and ninety-nine employees may also establish a policy committee.  Furthermore, an employer may establish multiple policy committees with the agreement of the union and employees.
"Section 134.1 (1) For the purposes of addressing health and safety matters that apply to the work, undertaking or business of an employer, every employer who normally employs directly three hundred or more employees shall establish a policy health and safety committee and, subject to section 135.1, select and appoint its members."

### Core Duties of the Policy Committee

The policy committee has a broad range of responsibilities aimed at promoting and maintaining a safe and healthy work environment. These duties include:

*   **Policy and Program Development:
"A policy committee (a) shall participate in the development of health and safety policies and programs..." This indicates that the committee plays a key role in shaping the overall health and safety strategy of the workplace.
*   **Addressing Health and Safety Concerns:
"(b) shall consider and expeditiously dispose of matters concerning health and safety raised by members of the committee or referred to it by a work place committee or a health and safety representative..." This highlights the committee's function as a forum for addressing employee concerns and escalating issues as needed.
*   **Hazard Prevention Program:
"(c) shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the prevention of hazards in the work place that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters..." This emphasizes the committee's role in proactively identifying and mitigating hazards, as well as ensuring employees are informed about safety procedures.
*   **Participation in Investigations and Inspections:
"(d) shall participate to the extent that it considers necessary in inquiries, investigations, studies and inspections pertaining to occupational health and safety..." This demonstrates the committee's involvement in ensuring thorough investigations of incidents and proactive inspections of the workplace.
*   **Personal Protective Equipment Program:
"(e) shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials..." This indicates the committee's role in ensuring employees have the necessary equipment to perform their jobs safely.
*   **Monitoring and Reporting:
"(g) shall monitor data on work accidents, injuries and health hazards..." This highlights the committee's responsibility for tracking safety performance and identifying trends.
*   **Planning and Implementation of Changes:
"(h) shall participate in the planning of the implementation and in the implementation of changes that might affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures." This shows the committee's role in ensuring that changes to the workplace are made with safety in mind.

### Limitations

It is important to note that a policy committee is specifically excluded from participating in investigations related to harassment and violence in the workplace.
"Marginal note: Investigation — harassment and violence (4.1) Despite paragraph (4)(d), a policy committee shall not participate in an investigation, other than an investigation under section 128 or 129, relating to an occurrence of harassment and violence in the..." This limitation is in place to ensure that investigations into harassment and violence are handled by specialized personnel.

question: What are the responsibilities of a workplace health and safety committee in a workplace with 20 or more employees, according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Responsibilities of a Workplace Health and Safety Committee (20+ Employees)

### Section 134.1(4) - General Duties of the Committee

According to Section 134.1(4) of the Canada Labour Code, a policy health and safety committee, established in workplaces with 20 or more employees, has a broad range of responsibilities. These duties are designed to proactively address and improve health and safety within the workplace.

#### Policy and Program Development
"A policy committee (a) shall participate in the development of health and safety policies and programs..."

This indicates that the committee plays a key role in creating the framework for health and safety practices within the workplace. This includes developing policies and programs to prevent hazards and promote a safe working environment.

#### Addressing Health and Safety Concerns
"(b) shall consider and expeditiously dispose of matters concerning health and safety raised by members of the committee or referred to it by a work place committee or a health and safety representative..."

This responsibility highlights the committee's role in addressing health and safety concerns raised by employees or representatives. The committee is expected to consider these matters promptly and find solutions.

#### Hazard Prevention and Education
"(c) shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the prevention of hazards in the work place that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters..."

This duty emphasizes the committee's involvement in preventing hazards and educating employees about health and safety. This includes developing and monitoring programs to address potential risks and ensuring employees have the knowledge to work safely.

#### Participation in Investigations and Inspections
"(d) shall participate to the extent that it considers necessary in inquiries, investigations, studies and inspections pertaining to occupational health and safety..."

The committee is required to participate in investigations, studies, and inspections related to occupational health and safety. This ensures that potential hazards are identified and addressed effectively.

#### Program for Personal Protective Equipment
"(e) shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials..."

This responsibility indicates that the committee is involved in developing and monitoring programs related to personal protective equipment (PPE). This ensures that employees have the necessary PPE to protect themselves from workplace hazards.

#### Monitoring and Planning
"(g) shall monitor data on work accidents, injuries and health..."
"(h) shall participate in the planning of the implementation and in the implementation of changes that might affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures."

These duties highlight the committee's role in monitoring workplace safety data and participating in the planning and implementation of changes to improve safety. This includes tracking accidents, injuries, and hazards, and working to implement changes that reduce risks.



### Section 134.1(7) - Meeting Requirements
"A policy committee shall meet during regular working hours at least quarterly and, if other meetings are required as a result of an emergency or other special circumstances, the committee shall meet as required during regular working hours or outside those hours."

This section specifies the minimum meeting frequency for the committee, ensuring regular communication and collaboration on health and safety matters. It also allows for additional meetings when necessary, such as in response to emergencies or special circumstances.
