question: What happens to an employer's administrative fee if it is overpaid, and what is the status of an unpaid administrative fee?
answer:
## Overpaid Administrative Fees

### Employer's Entitlement to Reimbursement

According to Section 251.131(2) of the Canada Labour Code,
"In the case of any overpayment, the employer is entitled to its reimbursement." This means that if an employer pays an administrative fee that exceeds the amount owed, they are entitled to have the excess amount returned to them.

## Status of Unpaid Administrative Fees

### Debt to Her Majesty

Section 251.131(3) clarifies the status of unpaid administrative fees. It states,
"An administrative fee constitutes a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and is recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act, including under subsection 251.13(1) and section 251.15." This indicates that an unpaid administrative fee is considered a debt owed to the Canadian government.

### Recovery Mechanisms

The text further explains how these debts can be recovered.
"...and is recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act, including under subsection 251.13(1) and section 251.15." This suggests that the government has various legal avenues to recover unpaid administrative fees, including through the Federal Court.

### Administrative Fee Calculation

Section 251.131(1) details how the administrative fee is calculated:
"...which is equal to the greater of $200 and 15% of the amounts indicated in the payment order or decision..." This means the fee is the higher of these two amounts.

### Payment of Administrative Fees

Section 251.131(2) also specifies that
"The employer is liable only for the administrative fee that is specified in a final decision and shall pay it — less any administrative fee paid under subsection 251.101(2) or 251.11(3) — to the Head." This indicates that the employer is only responsible for the fee specified in a final decision and that any previously paid fees may be deducted.

question: What happens to the money received by the Head under the Labour Standards division, and how are administrative fees handled?
answer:
## Disposition of Funds Received by the Head

### Labour Standards Suspense Account
"If the Head receives moneys under this Division, the Head shall deposit those moneys to the credit of the Receiver General in the account known as the “Labour Standards Suspense Account” or in any other special account created for the purposes of this section and may authorize payments out of that account to any employee or other person who is entitled to that money."

This passage from CLC-251.14 outlines the initial handling of funds received by the Head. The funds are deposited into a specific account, the "Labour Standards Suspense Account," managed by the Receiver General. This account serves as a holding place for money related to labour standards matters. The funds can then be used to make payments to eligible employees or other individuals as determined by the Labour Program.

### Administrative Fees

### Calculation and Application
"The following administrative fee will be added to the Payment Order when issued to the employer:  a fee of $200, or a fee of 15% of the total amount owed   Note: If the 15% of the total amount owed is more than $200, the Labour Program will apply that amount to the Payment Order along with the wages or other monies owed to the employee."

This section from LABOUR-STANDARDS-6_5 details the administrative fees associated with payment orders issued to employers. The fee is calculated as either a flat rate of \$200 or 15% of the total amount owed, whichever is greater. The Labour Program applies this fee to the payment order alongside the wages or other amounts due to the employee.

### Disposition of Administrative Fees
"...moneys that are equal to the administrative fees paid to the Head under this Part with respect to matters that are the subject of a final decision shall be debited from the account referred to in subsection (1) and credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund no later than the fiscal year following the fiscal year in which the final decision is made."

According to CLC-251.14, administrative fees collected are credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This means the money is directed to the general revenue of Canada, not retained by the Labour Program.

### Recovery of Administrative Fees
"An administrative fee constitutes a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and is recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act, including under subsection 251.13(1) and section 251.15."

CLC-251.131 clarifies that administrative fees are considered a debt owed to the Crown. This allows the government to pursue recovery of these fees through legal channels, such as the Federal Court, if necessary.

### Security and Return of Funds
"The Head, after a final decision has been made in respect of which security was given, (a) may apply, in whole or in part, the security given under subsection 251.101(2.1) or 251.11(3.1) toward any amounts — and, if the security was given by an employer, any administrative fee — owing under the final decision by the employer or a director of a corporation who gave the security; and (b) shall return the security or, if it was applied under paragraph (a), any part that remains after the amounts and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee have been paid."

CLC-251.132 explains how security (like a letter of credit) provided by an employer is handled. The Labour Program can use the security to cover outstanding amounts, including administrative fees. Any remaining security after settling the debt, including the administrative fee, is returned to the employer or director.

question: What happens to a payment order or Board order under the Canada Labour Code once it is filed in the Federal Court, and what are the implications for enforcement?
answer:
## Filing and Enforcement of Orders in Federal Court

### General Registration and Legal Effect

Section 251.15 states:
"On the filing of a copy of an order in the Federal Court under subsection (1) or (2), the order shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court."

This indicates that once a payment order or a Board order is filed in the Federal Court, it undergoes registration. This registration is crucial because it imbues the order with the same legal force and effect as a judgment issued by the Court. This means that the order becomes legally binding and enforceable in the same manner as a judgment.

### Enforcement Implications

Section 244(2) further clarifies the implications of registration:
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court."

This reinforces the point that the registered order can be used as the basis for legal proceedings.  This allows for effective enforcement of the order.  The ability to take proceedings "in respect of it" signifies that the order can be used to initiate legal actions to ensure compliance.

### Limitation on Filing

However, Section 251.15(1.1) outlines a limitation on filing:
"However, a payment order is not to be filed while it is or may be the subject of a review under subsection 251.101(1) or an appeal under subsection 251.101(7) or section 251.11 or if an order of the Board is made under paragraph 251.12(1)(a) relating to the payment order."

This means that filing a payment order in the Federal Court is restricted if it is currently under review or appeal, or if a Board order concerning the payment order is being made. This prevents premature or conflicting legal actions.

### Debt to Her Majesty

Section 251.15(6) also addresses the enforcement of orders related to debts owed to the Crown:
"The expenses to be paid in accordance with an order issued under paragraph (1)(d) constitute a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and are recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act."

This indicates that orders for costs incurred by the Board can be enforced as a debt owed to the Crown, providing a mechanism for recovering these expenses through the Federal Court or other appropriate legal avenues.

question: Can directors of a corporation be held personally liable for unpaid wages and other amounts owed to employees?
answer:
## Personal Liability of Directors for Unpaid Wages

### CLC-251.18: Joint and Several Liability

Section 251.18 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses the personal liability of directors for unpaid wages. It states:
"Section 251.18 Directors of a corporation are jointly and severally liable for wages and other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part, to a maximum amount equivalent to six months’ wages, to the extent that (a) the entitlement arose during the particular director’s incumbency; and (b) recovery of the amount from the corporation is impossible or unlikely."

This section establishes that directors are "jointly and severally liable" for employee wages. This means that employees can pursue legal action against one or more directors, or against all of them, to recover unpaid wages. Furthermore, the liability is capped at "a maximum amount equivalent to six months’ wages." The liability is contingent on two conditions: the entitlement must have occurred during the director's time on the board, and recovery from the corporation is either impossible or unlikely.

### CLC-251.19: Cooperative Corporations

Section 251.19 clarifies the applicability of this liability to cooperative corporations:
"Section 251.19 For the purposes of section 251.18 and subsection 257(3), cooperatives shall be deemed to be corporations."

This ensures that the provisions of section 251.18 apply to directors of cooperative corporations as well, extending the personal liability to this type of organizational structure.

In summary, based on CLC-251.18, directors of a corporation, including cooperative corporations, can be held personally liable for unpaid wages to employees under specific circumstances.

question: What are the responsibilities of an employer in Canada regarding the provision and maintenance of employee work records and information as per the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Employer Responsibilities Regarding Employee Work Records and Information in Canada

### Keeping of Records (Section 24 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations)

Section 24 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations outlines the comprehensive responsibilities of employers in maintaining employee records. 

#### Mandatory Records to be Kept
"Every employer shall make and keep a record in respect of each employee showing the date of commencement of employment and the date of termination of employment and shall keep such record for a period of at least 36 months after the date of termination of employment." This indicates that employers are required to document the start and end dates of employment for each employee and retain this information for a minimum of 36 months after the employment ends.

#### Detailed Information Required

The regulations specify a wide range of information that must be recorded for each employee. This includes:

*   **Personal Information:
"...the full name, address, Social Insurance Number, occupational classification and sex of the employee, and if the employee is under the age of 18 years, the age of the employee..." This highlights the need to collect and maintain basic personal details of employees.
*   **Wage Information:
"...the rate of wages, clearly indicating whether it is on an hourly, weekly, monthly or other basis, and the date and particulars of any change in the rate..." Employers must accurately record the wage rate and any changes to it.
*   **Hours Worked:
"...the hours worked each day, except where the employee is (i) excluded from the application of Division I of the Act by or under subsection 167(2) of the Act..." Employers are required to track the hours worked by each employee.
*   **Earnings Details:
"...the actual earnings, indicating the amounts paid each pay day, with a recording of the amounts paid for overtime, vacation pay, general holiday pay, personal leave pay, pay for leave for victims of family violence, bereavement leave pay, medical leave of absence pay, termination pay and severance pay..." Employers must meticulously record all earnings, including overtime and various types of leave pay.
*   **Deductions:
"...the payments made each pay day after deductions, with clear details of the deductions made..." Employers must provide a detailed breakdown of deductions made from employee paychecks.
*   **Leave Records:
"...with respect to any leave granted to the employee under Division VII of the Act, (i) the dates of commencement and termination, and of any interruption, of the leave, (ii) a copy of any notice concerning the leave or any interruption of the leave, and (iii) any documentation, including a copy of any medical certificate, that was provided by the employee in respect of the leave or interruption..." Employers must maintain records of all types of leave granted to employees, including medical leave.
*   **Work Schedules:
"...every work schedule and modification of a work schedule that is provided in writing to an employee..." Employers must maintain records of work schedules and any changes to them.

#### Record Retention Period
"Every employer shall keep for a period of at least three years after the expiration of the employer’s obligation under subsection 239.1(3) of the Act, the following information: (a) detailed reasons for an employee’s absence due to work-related illness or injury; (b) a copy of any certificate of a health care practitioner indicating that the employee is fit to return to work..." This indicates that employers must retain records of employee absences due to illness or injury for at least three years after the obligation under the Act expires.

### Sharing Records with the Labour Program (Section 8_3 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations)

While not explicitly detailing the record-keeping requirements, this section highlights the employer's obligation to cooperate with the Labour Program.
"The Labour Program may ask to see your employment and payroll records when inspecting your workplace or investigating a complaint." This implies that employers must be prepared to provide the Labour Program with access to employee records when requested. Failure to do so may result in enforcement actions.

### Further Specific Duties of Employer (Section 125 of the Canada Labour Code)

Section 125 of the Canada Labour Code outlines further specific duties of employers, which indirectly relate to record-keeping.

#### Hazardous Substances
"...ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards..." This implies that employers must maintain records related to the presence and control of hazardous substances in the workplace.

#### Hazardous Products
"...other than hazardous products, are identified in the manner prescribed..." This indicates the need for records related to the identification and handling of hazardous products.

#### Exposure Assessment
"...to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..." This suggests that employers must maintain records of exposure assessments conducted in the workplace.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code and Regulations place a significant burden on employers to maintain detailed and accurate records of their employees. These records are essential for ensuring compliance with labour standards, protecting employee rights, and facilitating investigations by the Labour Program.

{"id": "CLC-253", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Information and Returns: Notice to furnish information", "section": "253"}, "text": "Section 253 (1) Where the Head is authorized to require a person to furnish information under this Part or the regulations, the Head may require the information to be furnished by a notice to that effect served by personal service, by registered mail addressed to the latest known address of the addressee, or by any other means prescribed by regulation, and that person (a) if the notice is sent by registered mail, is deemed to have received the notice on the seventh day after the day on which it was mailed; and (b) shall furnish the information within such reasonable time as is specified in the notice. Marginal note: Proof of service (2) A certificate purporting to be signed by the Head certifying that a notice was sent by registered mail or by any other means prescribed by regulation to the addressee, accompanied by a true copy of the notice and by an identifying post office certificate of the registration or other proof, prescribed by regulation, that the notice has been sent or received, is admissible in evidence and is proof of the statements contained in the certificate, without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate. Marginal note: Proof of failure to comply (3) Where the Head is authorized to require a person to furnish information under this Part or the regulations, a certificate of the Head certifying that the information has not been furnished is admissible in evidence and in the absence of any evidence to the contrary is proof of the statements contained in it. Marginal note: Proof of documents (4) A certificate of the Head certifying that a document annexed to it is a document or a true copy of the document made by or on behalf of the Head shall be admitted in evidence and has the same force and effect as if it had been proven in the ordinary way. Marginal note: Proof of authority (5) A certificate under this section signed or purporting to be signed by the Head is admissible in evidence without proof of the Head’s appointment or signature. Marginal note: Statutory Instruments Act (6) The Statutory Instruments Act does not apply in respect of notices referred to in subsection (1). R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 253 1993, c. 42, s. 39 2017, c. 20, s. 374 2018, c. 27, s. 609"

question: How can the Head require a person to furnish information under this Part or the regulations, and what are the implications of the methods used for serving notices?
answer:
## Methods for the Head to Require Information Furnishing

### Section 253(1) - General Requirements for Service
"Where the Head is authorized to require a person to furnish information under this Part or the regulations, the Head may require the information to be furnished by a notice to that effect served by personal service, by registered mail addressed to the latest known address of the addressee, or by any other means prescribed by regulation..."

This section outlines the primary methods the Head can use to request information. These methods include:

*   **Personal Service:** Delivering the notice directly to the individual.
*   **Registered Mail:** Sending the notice via registered mail to the individual's last known address.
*   **Other Means Prescribed by Regulation:** Utilizing any other method authorized by regulations.

### Section 253(1)(a) - Proof of Registered Mail Service
"...that person (a) if the notice is sent by registered mail, is deemed to have received the notice on the seventh day after the day on which it was mailed..."

This subsection clarifies the timeline for when registered mail is considered delivered. It states that a person is deemed to have received the notice seven days after it was mailed.

### Section 253(2) - Proof of Service Certificates
"A certificate purporting to be signed by the Head certifying that a notice was sent by registered mail or by any other means prescribed by regulation to the addressee, accompanied by a true copy of the notice and by an identifying post office certificate of the registration or other proof, prescribed by regulation, that the notice has been sent or received, is admissible in evidence and is proof of the statements contained in the certificate, without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate."

This section provides a mechanism for proving that a notice was indeed sent. It states that a certificate from the Head (or someone authorized by the Head) detailing the method of service, along with supporting documentation (like a post office certificate), is admissible as evidence. This certificate serves as proof of the facts stated within it, even without verifying the signature of the person who signed it.

### Section 253(3) - Proof of Failure to Comply
"Where the Head is authorized to require a person to furnish information under this Part or the regulations, a certificate of the Head certifying that the information has not been furnished is admissible in evidence and in the absence of any evidence to the contrary is proof of the statements contained in it."

This section allows the Head to provide a certificate stating that the requested information has not been provided. This certificate is admissible as evidence and is considered proof that the information was not furnished, unless there is evidence to the contrary.

### Section 253(4) - Proof of Documents Annexed to Notices
"A certificate of the Head certifying that a document annexed to it is a document or a true copy of the document made by or on behalf of the Head shall be admitted in evidence and has the same force and effect as if it had been proven in the ordinary way."

This section allows the Head to certify that a document attached to a notice is authentic. This certificate is admissible as evidence and has the same legal weight as if the document had been proven through standard means.

### Section 253(5) - Proof of Authority
"A certificate under this section signed or purporting to be signed by the Head is admissible in evidence without proof of the Head’s appointment or signature."

This section allows a certificate signed by the Head (or appearing to be signed by the Head) to be used as evidence without needing to prove the Head's appointment or signature.

### Section 253(6) - Exemption of Statutory Instruments Act
"The Statutory Instruments Act does not apply in respect of notices referred to in subsection (1)."

This section clarifies that the Statutory Instruments Act does not apply to notices issued under this section.

(r) maintain all installed guards, guard-rails, barricades and fences in accordance with prescribed standards; (s) ensure that each employee is made aware of every known or foreseeable health or safety hazard in the area where the employee works; (t) ensure that the machinery, equipment and tools used by the employees in the course of their employment meet prescribed health, safety and ergonomic standards and are safe under all conditions of their intended use; (u) ensure that the work place, work spaces and procedures meet prescribed ergonomic standards; (v) adopt and implement prescribed safety codes and safety standards; (w) ensure that every person granted access to the work place by the employer is familiar with and uses in the prescribed circumstances and manner all prescribed safety materials, equipment, devices and clothing; (x) comply with every oral or written direction given to the employer by the Head or the Board concerning the health and safety of employees; (y) ensure that the activities of every person granted access to the work place do not endanger the health and safety of employees; (z) ensure that employees who have supervisory or managerial responsibilities are adequately trained in health and safety and are informed of the responsibilities they have under this Part where they act on behalf of their employer; (z.01) ensure that members of policy and work place committees and health and safety representatives receive the prescribed training in health and safety and are informed of their responsibilities under this Part; (z.02) respond as soon as possible to reports made by employees under paragraph 126(1)(g); (z.03) develop, implement and monitor, in consultation with the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, with the work place committee or the health and safety representative, a prescribed program for the prevention of hazards in the work place appropriate to its size and the nature of the hazards in it that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters; (z.04) where the program referred to in paragraph (z.03) does not cover certain hazards unique to a work place, develop, implement and monitor, in consultation with the work place committee or the health and safety representative, a prescribed program for the prevention of those hazards that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters related to those hazards; (z.05) consult the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, the work place committee or the health and safety representative to plan the implementation of changes that might affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures; (z.06) consult the work place committee or the health and safety representative in the implementation of changes that might affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures; (z.07) ensure the availability in the work place of premises, equipment and personnel necessary for the operation of the policy and work place committees; (z.08) cooperate with the policy and work place committees or the health and safety representative in the execution of their duties under this Part; (z.09) develop health and safety policies and programs in consultation with the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, with the work place committee or the health and safety representative; (z.14) take all reasonable care to ensure that all of the persons granted access to the work place, other than the employer’s employees, are informed of every known or foreseeable health or safety hazard to which they are likely to be exposed in the work place; question: What are the responsibilities of an employer in terms of providing information to employees about their rights and obligations, and employment details?
answer:
## Employer Responsibilities Regarding Information Provision

Here's a breakdown of an employer's responsibilities concerning information provision to employees, based on the provided documents:

### Employment Statements

**Employment Statement Requirements:
"Employers are prohibited from treating an employee as if they were not their employee. A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer."

This indicates a fundamental responsibility to correctly classify employees and avoid misclassification.
"The statement must include the information that is listed in section 3.1 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations. Employers can use the Employment Statement template made available online. Employers are not required to use this template and  can provide the information through other written documents. For example, the  information can be provided in a:  letter of job offer contract of employment policy  manual collective  agreement..."

This section outlines the mandatory information that must be included in an employment statement. It also provides flexibility in the format of the statement, allowing employers to use templates or other written documents.

**Timing and Record Keeping:
"The statement must be given to your employees within the first 30 days of their employment.  If you make any change to an employee’s statement, you must send them an updated copy within 30 days of making the change."

This highlights the importance of providing the employment statement promptly upon hiring and ensuring updates are provided in a timely manner whenever changes occur.
"...statements must be kept for 36 months after employment ends. Upon request, an employee must be provided additional copies of their statement."

This emphasizes the employer's obligation to maintain records of employment statements for a specified period and to provide copies to employees upon request.

### Health and Safety Information

**General Information:
"(d) make readily available to employees, in printed and electronic form, (i) a copy of this Part and a copy of the regulations made under this Part that apply to the work place, (ii) a statement of the employer’s general policy concerning the health and safety at work of employees, and (iii) any other information related to health and safety that is prescribed or that may be specified by the Head..."

This section mandates that employers make health and safety information readily available to employees in both printed and electronic formats. This includes the relevant sections of the Canada Labour Code and associated regulations, the employer's health and safety policy, and any other prescribed health and safety information.

**Hazardous Substances:
"(e) subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act..."

This section specifically requires employers to provide safety data sheets (SDS) for hazardous products to which employees may be exposed.

**Emergency Information:
"Section 125.2 (1) An employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls that activity, provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency."

This section outlines the employer's responsibility to provide safety data sheets to medical professionals in emergency situations.

### Other Information
"(f) if the information referred to in any of subparagraphs (d)(i) to (iii) is made available in electronic form, ensure that employees receive appropriate training to enable them to have access to the information and, on the request of an employee, make a printed copy of the information available..."

This indicates that if information is provided electronically, employers must ensure employees are trained to access it and provide printed copies upon request.

In summary, employers have a comprehensive responsibility to provide employees with essential information regarding their employment terms, health and safety, and potential hazards in the workplace. This includes providing employment statements, making health and safety information readily available, and ensuring employees have access to safety data sheets for hazardous products.

question: What information must an employer provide to an employee in writing at the time of making a payment of wages?
answer:
## Employer Requirements for Wage Statements

### Section 254 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 254 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the specific information an employer must provide to an employee in writing at the time of making any payment of wages. 

**Required Information:
"An employer shall, at the time of making any payment of wages to an employee, furnish the employee with a statement in writing setting out (a) the period for which the payment is made; (b) the number of hours for which the payment is made; (c) the rate of wages; (d) details of the deductions made from the wages; and (e) the actual sum being received by the employee."

This section mandates a detailed written statement that includes several key components. The statement must clearly indicate the timeframe covered by the payment ("the period for which the payment is made"), the number of hours worked (
"...the number of hours for which the payment is made..."), the hourly or overall wage rate ("the rate of wages"), a breakdown of any deductions ("details of the deductions made from the wages"), and the final amount the employee receives ("the actual sum being received by the employee"). 

This requirement ensures transparency and allows employees to verify the accuracy of their pay.

IPG-060_2:

{"id": "IPG-060_2", "type": "Interpretations, Policies and Guidelines", "title": "Deductions from wages or other amounts - IPG-060", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**When a deduction is found to have been authorized in writing pursuant to paragraph 254.1(2)(c) of the Code** Subsection 254.1(1) prohibits an employer from making deductions from wages or other amounts except under specific circumstances as set out in subsection 254.1(2). One of these specific circumstances [paragraph 254.1(2)(c)] is when the deductions are "amounts authorized in writing by the employee". Paragraph 254.1(2)(c), "amounts authorized in writing by the employee", requires a written authorization by the employee consenting to the deduction of a specific amount. For every deduction made, the authorization must be in writing, specify a particular amount, and be given in a way that is truly consensual. Where it is found that the deduction of a particular amount has been authorized in writing by the employee, it must also be confirmed whether the authorization was truly consented to by the employee.  **Whether the timing of the authorization has an impact on the validity of the deduction** General blanket authorizations in employment contracts, with or without specific amounts, may operate to assign responsibility or liability to the employee. However, the corresponding deduction requires a specific authorization. Whether the authorization for deduction is signed before, at the time of, or after the deduction is made is not a relevant factor on its own. A consent for wage deduction made at the time of or after an occurrence is more likely to be accepted than one which is made a considerable period before the deduction. The more specific and timely the authorization is to the actual occurrence the more likely it would be considered valid."

question: Under what conditions can an employer make deductions from an employee's wages or other amounts due to them?
answer:
## Conditions for Employer Deductions from Employee Wages

### Permitted Deductions According to the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code (CLC) outlines specific conditions under which an employer can make deductions from an employee's wages or other amounts due to them. Section 254.1 of the Code details these permitted deductions.

#### General Rule and Permitted Deductions
"No employer shall make deductions from wages or other amounts due to an employee, except as permitted by or under this section." This sets the foundational rule: deductions are generally prohibited. However, the Code specifies several exceptions.

The permitted deductions are:

*   **Deductions required by law:
"(a) those required by a federal or provincial Act or regulations made thereunder..." This covers deductions mandated by federal or provincial legislation, such as income taxes and employment insurance premiums.
*   **Deductions authorized by a court order or collective agreement:
"(b) those authorized by a court order or a collective agreement or other document signed by a trade union on behalf of the employee..." This includes deductions mandated by court orders (e.g., garnishment for child support) or agreed upon through collective bargaining.
*   **Deductions authorized in writing by the employee:** "(c) amounts authorized in writing by the employee." This is a crucial exception, allowing deductions if the employee provides explicit written consent.
*   **Recovery of overpayments:** "(d) overpayments of wages by the employer." This allows employers to recover wages that were accidentally overpaid to an employee.
*   **Other amounts prescribed by regulation:** "(e) other amounts prescribed by regulation." This allows for deductions specified in regulations made under the Code.

### Specific Restrictions and Limitations

While the Code permits deductions under certain conditions, it also includes restrictions.

#### Prohibition on Deductions for Property Damage
"Notwithstanding paragraph (2)(c), no employer shall, pursuant to that paragraph, make a deduction in respect of damage to property, or loss of money or property, if any person other than the employee had access to the property or money in question." This is a significant limitation. Even with written authorization, an employer cannot deduct for damage to property or loss of money/property if someone other than the employee had access to it. The employer would need to pursue recovery through civil court in such cases.

#### Importance of Written Authorization

The documents consistently emphasize the need for written authorization for deductions.
"For every deduction made, the authorization must be in writing, specify a particular amount, and be given in a way that is truly consensual." This highlights that a verbal agreement is not sufficient; a written agreement is required.

### Additional Considerations

The documents also highlight important considerations regarding the timing and nature of the authorization.
"**Whether the timing of the authorization has an impact on the validity of the deduction** General blanket authorizations in employment contracts, with or without specific amounts, may operate to assign responsibility or liability to the employee. However, the corresponding deduction requires a specific authorization. Whether the authorization for deduction is signed before, at the time of, or after the deduction is made is not a relevant factor on its own. A consent for wage deduction made at the time of or after an occurrence is more likely to be accepted than one which is made a considerable period before the deduction. The more specific and timely the authorization is to the actual occurrence the more likely it would be considered valid." This indicates that while a blanket authorization might be valid, specific authorizations tied to the actual deduction are more likely to be upheld.

### Employer's Responsibility
"The employer must use the funds deducted for the purposes authorized by the employee." This emphasizes that the employer is obligated to use the deducted funds as agreed upon with the employee.

question: What happens when multiple employers with common control operate federal works, undertakings, or businesses, and how are they held liable for employee entitlements?
answer:
## Combining Federal Works, Undertakings, and Businesses Under the Canada Labour Code

### Minister's Order for Combined Liability

Section 255(1) of the Canada Labour Code addresses situations where multiple employers share common control or direction over associated or related federal works, undertakings, and businesses. In such cases, the Minister has the authority to issue an order declaring these employers and the federal entities they operate to be a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking, or business. 

>
"Where associated or related federal works, undertakings and businesses are operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Minister may, after affording to the employers a reasonable opportunity to make representations, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

This provision allows for a streamlined approach to applying labour standards when multiple entities are intertwined in the operation of a federal enterprise. The Minister's order serves to consolidate responsibility and ensure consistent application of the Code.

### Joint and Several Liability for Employee Entitlements

Section 255(2) outlines the liability of employers operating under a Minister's order. It states that the employers subject to the order are jointly and severally liable to the employees working in the federal works, undertakings, and businesses covered by the order.

>
"Where an order is made under subsection (1), the employers to which it applies are jointly and severally liable to the employees employed in the federal works, undertakings and businesses to which the order applies for overtime pay, vacation pay, holiday pay and other wages or amounts to which the employees are entitled under this Part."

This means that employees have the option of pursuing a claim for unpaid wages or other entitlements against any one or all of the employers named in the order. The liability is shared, but each employer can be held responsible for the full amount owed. This provision is crucial for protecting employee rights when multiple employers are involved in the operation of a federal enterprise.

question: What are the consequences for an individual or an employer who contravenes a provision of the Canada Labour Code or the regulations, or discriminates against a person for providing information or testifying in proceedings?
answer:
## Consequences for Contravening the Canada Labour Code

### General Offences by Persons (Section 101)
"Subject to section 100, every person other than an employer or a trade union who contravenes or fails to comply with any provision of this Part other than section 50, 94 or 95 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars."

This section outlines the consequences for individuals who violate the Canada Labour Code, excluding employers and trade unions. The penalty is a fine of up to \$1,000 upon summary conviction.

### Offences by Employers and Trade Unions (Section 102)
"Subject to section 100, every employer or trade union who or that contravenes or fails to comply with any provision of this Part other than section 50, 94 or 95 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars."

This section specifies the consequences for employers and trade unions who violate the Canada Labour Code. The penalty is a fine of up to \$10,000 upon summary conviction.

### Offences Related to Testimony and Information (Section 147)
"Section 147 No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

Section 147 directly addresses the prohibition against employers taking adverse actions against employees for exercising their rights under the Canada Labour Code. It explicitly states that an employer cannot
"...dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration..." because the employee has
"...testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part..." or
"...provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer..." This indicates that employers face legal repercussions for retaliating against employees who provide information or testify in accordance with the Code.

### Abuse of Rights (Section 147.1)
"Section 147.1 (1) An employer may, after all the investigations and appeals have been exhausted by the employee who has exercised rights under sections 128 and 129, take disciplinary action against the employee who the employer can demonstrate has wilfully abused those rights."

This section introduces a specific exception to the protection afforded by Section 147. It allows an employer to take disciplinary action against an employee who has "wilfully abused" their rights under the Canada Labour Code, but only after all investigations and appeals have been completed. This suggests that while employees have strong protections, they are not immune from consequences if they misuse their rights.

## Consequences for Contravening Regulations (Section 273)
"Section 273 Every person or department that contravenes or fails to comply with a provision, direction, order or condition designated by regulations made under paragraph 270(1)(a) commits a violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations."

This section outlines the consequences for violating regulations made under the Canada Labour Code. The penalty is determined by the regulations themselves, indicating that the severity of the penalty can vary depending on the specific regulation violated.

## Liability of Parties to Violation (Section 274)
"Section 274 If a corporation or a department commits a violation, any of the following persons who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in the commission of the violation is a party to the violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations, whether or not the corporation or department has been proceeded against in accordance with this Part: (a) any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation; (b) any senior official in the department; or (c) any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department."

This section clarifies that liability for violations can extend beyond the corporation or department itself to individuals who directed, authorized, or participated in the violation. The penalty is determined by the regulations and applies to officers, directors, agents, senior officials, and other individuals with managerial or supervisory roles.

question: What are the key considerations for instituting proceedings in respect of an offence under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART III - Standard Hours, Wages, Vacations and Holidays?
answer:
## Key Considerations for Instituting Proceedings for an Offence Under Part III of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 257(2) - Time Limit for Proceedings
"...in respect of an offence under this Part may be instituted at any time within but not later than three years after the time when the subject-matter of the proceedings arose."

This section establishes a crucial time limit for initiating proceedings related to an offence under Part III of the Canada Labour Code.  The timeframe is
"...within but not later than three years after the time when the subject-matter of the proceedings arose." This means that legal action must be commenced within three years of when the violation occurred.  Failure to do so may prevent the prosecution of the offence.

### Section 257(3) - Minister's Consent for Corporate Directors
"No proceeding against a director of a corporation in respect of an offence under this Part shall be instituted except with the consent of the Minister."

This section introduces a specific requirement when proceedings are directed against a director of a corporation. It states that
"No proceeding against a director of a corporation in respect of an offence under this Part shall be instituted except with the consent of the Minister." This implies that the Minister has the authority to grant or deny permission for legal action against corporate directors, suggesting a level of oversight and potentially a consideration of the implications of such action.

### Section 257(1) - Scope of Complaints/Information
"A complaint or information under this Part may relate to one or more offences by one employer in respect of one or more of his employees."

This section clarifies the scope of complaints or information that can be brought forward. It states that
"A complaint or information under this Part may relate to one or more offences by one employer in respect of one or more of his employees." This means that a single complaint can encompass multiple violations committed by the same employer against different employees, or multiple violations committed against the same employee. This broadens the potential scope of legal action.

question: What are the potential consequences for an employer who has been convicted of an offence under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART III - Standard Hours, Wages, Vacations and Holidays), in relation to employee wages and employment status?
answer:
## Consequences for Employers Convicted of Offences Under the Canada Labour Code (Part III)

Here's a breakdown of the potential consequences for employers convicted of offences under Part III of the Canada Labour Code, specifically relating to employee wages and employment status, based on the provided documents.

### General Offences and Penalties

**Section 101 (CLC-101)** outlines the general offences and penalties for employers and trade unions who contravene provisions of the Canada Labour Code, excluding specific sections related to wages, hours, vacation, and holidays (sections 50, 94, or 95).

>
"...to section 100, every employer or trade union who or that contravenes or fails to comply with any provision of this Part other than section 50, 94 or 95 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars."

This indicates that an employer found in violation of the Canada Labour Code (Part III) can face a fine of up to \$10,000 upon a summary conviction.

**Section 148 (CLC-148)** provides a more extensive range of penalties, particularly for offences that result in death, serious illness, or serious injury to an employee.

>
"Section 148 (1) Subject to this section, every person who contravenes a provision of this Part is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $100,000."

This section specifies that a conviction on indictment can result in a fine of up to \$1,000,000 or imprisonment for up to two years, or both. A summary conviction carries a fine of up to \$100,000.

### Specific Offences and Penalties Related to Wages and Employment Status

**Section 256 (CLC-256)** details offences related to contravening provisions of the Canada Labour Code, including those concerning wages, hours of work, and other employment conditions.

>
"Section 256 (1) Every person is guilty of an offence who (a) contravenes any provision of this Part or the regulations, other than a provision of Division IX, subsection 239.1(2), 239.2(1), 251.001(9) or 252(2) or any regulation made under section 227 or paragraph 264(1)(a) or (a.1); (b) contravenes any order made under this Part or the regulations; or (c) discharges, threatens to discharge or otherwise discriminates against a person because that person (i) has testified or is about to testify in any proceedings or inquiry taken or had under this Part, or (ii) has given any information to the Minister or the Head regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of an employee."

This section explicitly mentions that contravening provisions related to wages, hours of work, annual vacation, or conditions of work constitutes an offence. Furthermore, it addresses the consequences of discharging, threatening to discharge, or otherwise discriminating against an employee for testifying or providing information about their wages, hours, vacation, or working conditions.

**Section 256 (1.1) (CLC-256)** outlines the fine structure for offences under Section 256, differentiating between corporations and other individuals.

>
"(1.1) Every person who is guilty of an offence under subsection (1) is liable on summary conviction (a) in the case of an employer that is a corporation, (i) for a first offence, to a fine of not more than $50,000, (ii) for a second offence, to a fine of not more than $100,000, and (iii) for each subsequent offence, to a fine of not more than $250,000; and (b) in all other cases, (i) for a first offence, to a fine of not more than $10,000, (ii) for a second offence, to a fine of not more than $20,000, and (iii) for each subsequent offence, to a fine of not more than $50,000."

This provides a tiered fine structure based on the number of offences committed. Corporations face significantly higher fines than individuals.

**Section 256 (2) (CLC-256)** specifies that employers who contravene provisions of Division IX, subsection 239.1(2) or 239.2(1) or any regulation made under section 227 are guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and liable to a fine of not more than \$250,000. This directly relates to offences concerning wages and other employment conditions.

**Section 256 (3) (CLC-256)** addresses the failure to keep or provide records related to employment conditions, imposing a fine of not more than \$1,000 for each day the failure continues. This is directly relevant to ensuring transparency and accountability regarding wages and working conditions.

In summary, an employer convicted of an offence under Part III of the Canada Labour Code faces potential consequences including fines ranging from \$1,000 to \$1,000,000 (depending on the severity of the offence and whether it's a summary conviction or conviction on indictment), imprisonment, and significant financial penalties for corporations. Furthermore, employers can be penalized for discriminatory actions against employees who report violations of wage and employment standards, and for failing to maintain required records.

question: What are the consequences for an employer that fails to comply with an order of a convicting court made under section 258 of the Canada Labour Code, and how can penalties be recovered?
answer:
## Consequences for Non-Compliance with Section 258 Orders

### Summary of Consequences

Section 259 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the consequences for an employer who fails to comply with an order issued by a court after being convicted of an offence under section 258. The primary consequence is a fine.

### Fine for Failure to Comply
"An employer that fails to comply with an order of a convicting court made under section 258 is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and liable to a fine of not more than $1,000 for each day during which the failure continues."

This indicates that the employer is considered to have committed an offence and will be fined for each day the order is not followed. This fine is a summary conviction offence.

### Recovery of Penalties

Section 259.1 addresses the recovery of penalties when a person is convicted of an offence under this Part and the fine is not paid.
"Where a person is convicted of an offence under this Part and the fine that is imposed is not paid when required, the prosecutor may, by filing the conviction, enter as a judgment the amount of the fine and costs, if any, in a superior court of the province in which the trial was held, and the judgment is enforceable against the person in the same manner as if it were a judgment rendered against the person in that court in civil proceedings."

This section allows the prosecutor to pursue the outstanding fine as a civil judgment in a superior court. This means the fine can be recovered through standard civil court procedures, ensuring the employer is held accountable for the unpaid penalty.

question: Under what circumstances can the identity of a person making a complaint be disclosed if they have requested that it be kept confidential?
answer:
## Section 260: Offences and Punishment: Identity of Complainants

### Confidentiality of Identity

Section 260(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the conditions under which the identity of a complainant can be disclosed, even if the complainant has requested that their name and identity be withheld. The section states:
"If a person makes a complaint under this Part and requests that their name and identity be withheld, their name and identity must not be disclosed unless (a) the disclosure is necessary for the purposes of a prosecution; (b) the Head determines that the disclosure is in the public interest; or (c) the Head determines that the disclosure is necessary for the investigation of the complaint to be carried out and the complainant consents to the disclosure in writing."

This indicates that the default position is to maintain the confidentiality of the complainant's identity. However, there are specific exceptions where disclosure is permitted. 

The exceptions are:

*   **(a) Necessity for Prosecution:** Disclosure is allowed if it is "necessary for the purposes of a prosecution." This suggests that if legal proceedings are initiated, the complainant's identity may need to be revealed.
*   **(b) Public Interest:** Disclosure is permitted if
"...the Head determines that the disclosure is in the public interest..." This provides a broad exception, allowing for disclosure if it serves a greater societal good.
*   **(c) Necessity for Investigation and Complainant Consent:** Disclosure is allowed if
"...the Head determines that the disclosure is necessary for the investigation of the complaint to be carried out and the complainant consents to the disclosure in writing." This exception highlights the importance of the complainant's consent, even if disclosure is deemed necessary for the investigation. The complainant must explicitly agree to the disclosure in writing for it to be permissible under this condition.

Section 260(2) further clarifies that if a complainant refuses to provide written consent for disclosure under the conditions outlined in (1)(c), the Head may deem the complaint to be withdrawn. This underscores the importance of the complainant's willingness to consent to disclosure.

Section 261 explicitly addresses the impact of this Part on an employee's right to pursue civil remedies for unpaid wages. It states:
"Section 261 No civil remedy of an employee against his employer for arrears of wages is suspended or affected by this Part."

This means that the existence of the procedures outlined in this Part – such as the Head issuing a payment order – does not prevent an employee from pursuing a civil lawsuit against their employer to recover unpaid wages. The Part provides an alternative mechanism for addressing unpaid wages, but it does not eliminate the employee's right to seek redress through the civil court system.

### Summary

In essence, this Part does not remove or hinder an employee's ability to seek civil remedies for unpaid wages. It operates alongside existing civil remedies, offering an additional avenue for resolution.

## Ministerial Orders in the Canada Labour Code

### General Authority for Ministerial Orders

Section 262 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the authority of the Minister to issue orders. It states:
"Section 262 Where by this Part or the regulations the Minister is authorized to make any order in respect of any matter, the order may be made to apply generally or in particular cases or to apply to classes of employees or industrial..."

This section explicitly confirms that the Minister has the power to create orders with varying scopes. The phrase "apply generally" indicates the Minister can issue orders that have broad applicability, affecting a wide range of situations or entities. Conversely, the phrase
"...in particular cases or to apply to classes of employees or industrial establishments." demonstrates the Minister's ability to tailor orders to specific circumstances or groups.

### Scope of Application

The text highlights the flexibility in how these orders can be applied. The Minister isn't limited to a single scope; they can choose to make an order that is either universally applicable or targeted towards specific situations or groups. This flexibility allows the Minister to address a wide range of labour-related matters effectively.

question: What is the purpose of the Governor in Council's regulatory power under section 263 of the Canada Labour Code, and what kind of projects can they establish?
answer:
## Purpose of Governor in Council's Regulatory Power under Section 263

### Establishing and Operating Pilot Projects

The purpose of the Governor in Council's regulatory power under section 263 of the Canada Labour Code is to facilitate the establishment and operation of pilot projects. These projects are designed for
"...testing which possible amendments to this Part or the regulations made under this Part would improve and better protect employees’ rights under this Part..."

This means the Governor in Council can create temporary, controlled environments to evaluate potential changes to the Canada Labour Code and its associated regulations. The goal is to assess the impact of these changes before implementing them broadly.

### Types of Projects

The section specifies that the pilot projects can be related to
"...the establishment and operation of one or more pilot projects..." This indicates that the Governor in Council can establish multiple pilot projects simultaneously, potentially focusing on different aspects of the Canada Labour Code or different types of workplaces.

Furthermore, the Governor in Council has the authority to regulate
"...the manner in which and the extent to which any provision of this Part or the regulations made under this Part applies to a pilot project and adapting any such provision for the purposes of that application." This highlights the flexibility of the regulatory power, allowing for tailored approaches to testing specific provisions within the pilot projects.

The section also includes a provision regarding the repeal of regulations made under section 263, stating that they are repealed on the fifth anniversary of the day on which they come into force, unless repealed earlier. This suggests that pilot projects are intended to be temporary and that the regulations governing them are not intended to be permanent.

question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make in order to carry out the purposes of a Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART III - Standard Hours, Wages, Vacations and Holidays)?
answer:
## Regulations Regarding Standard Hours, Wages, Vacations, and Holidays (Part III)

### General Authority for Regulations

Section 264(1) of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to
"...make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Part..." This establishes the broad basis for the types of regulations that can be enacted.

### Specific Areas of Regulation

Section 264(1) then lists a comprehensive set of specific areas where regulations can be made. These include:

#### 1. Record Keeping
"(a) requiring employers to keep records of wages, vacations, holidays and overtime of employees and of other particulars relevant to the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof..."

This indicates that regulations can mandate specific record-keeping requirements for employers related to wages, vacations, holidays, and overtime, all crucial aspects of Part III.

#### 2. Exclusions from Application
"(a.1) requiring employers to keep records relevant to the purposes of this Part in respect of persons who are excluded under subsection 167(1.2) from the application of all or any of this Part..."

This allows for regulations to specify record-keeping requirements for employers regarding excluded employees, ensuring that even those not fully covered by Part III still have relevant records maintained.

#### 3. Information Provision to the Head
"(a.2) respecting the information that an employer must provide to the Head for the purpose of establishing that the performance of activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) fulfils the requirements of a program referred to in that subsection, and the circumstances in which an employer must provide it..."

This enables regulations to dictate the information employers must provide to the Head to demonstrate compliance with specific programs, which is relevant to the overall objectives of Part III.

#### 4. Calculation of Wages
"(d) for calculating and determining wages received by an employee in respect of his employment, including the monetary value of remuneration other than money and, for the purposes of any provision or provisions of this Part specified in the regulations, the regular rate of wages of employees..."

This is a core function of Part III, and regulations can specify how wages are calculated, including non-monetary compensation and the determination of regular wage rates.

#### 5. Hourly Wage Calculation
"(e) for calculating and determining the regular rate of wages, on an hourly basis, of employees who are paid on any basis of time other than hourly or who are not paid solely on a basis of time..."

This allows for regulations to address the specific calculation of hourly wages for employees with non-standard pay schedules, ensuring fair compensation.

#### 6. Payment of Wages to the Head
"(i) providing for the payment of any wages of an employee to the Head or to another person in the event that the employee cannot be found or in any other case..."

This enables regulations to outline procedures for the payment of wages to the Head or another designated party when an employee is unable to be located, ensuring that wages are ultimately paid.

#### 7. Notification to Employees
"(h) requiring an employer in any industrial establishment to notify employees, by the publication of such notices, in such manner as may be prescribed, of (i) the provisions of this Part or any regulation or order made under this Part, (ii) the particulars of hours of work, including the hours at which shifts change, (iii) the particulars of rest periods and meal periods, and (iv) other matters related to hours and conditions of work of employees..."

This allows for regulations to mandate the notification of employees regarding the provisions of Part III, including details about working hours, rest periods, and meal periods.

#### 8. Establishment of Consultative Committees
"(j.1) prescribing the circumstances and conditions for the purposes of subsection 251.01(3)..."

This allows for regulations to establish consultative or advisory committees to advise the Minister on matters related to the administration of Part III.

In summary, the Governor in Council has broad authority to create regulations under Part III of the Canada Labour Code to address a wide range of issues related to standard hours, wages, vacations, and holidays, ensuring consistent application and addressing specific circumstances within the labour market.

question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council direct that a part of the Canada Labour Code (PART III - Standard Hours, Wages, Vacations and Holidays) applies to certain employment?
answer:
## Application of Canada Labour Code Part III to Provincial Crown Corporations

### Section 121.1
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section outlines the primary circumstance under which the Governor in Council can direct the application of Part III of the Canada Labour Code. Specifically, it applies to employment within corporations that are agents of the Crown in a province and whose activities are regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This suggests a specific context related to nuclear safety and control, where the Governor in Council has the power to extend labour code provisions.

### Section 265
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section is very similar to Section 121.1, reinforcing the power of the Governor in Council to direct the application of Part III to specific employment situations within Crown corporations regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. It essentially reiterates the same condition for application.

### Section 266
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

While Section 266 focuses on exclusion, it further emphasizes the Governor in Council's authority to determine the scope of Part III's application to these specific Crown corporations. The ability to both include and exclude provisions demonstrates a significant level of control over labour standards within these entities.

In summary, the Governor in Council can direct that Part III of the Canada Labour Code applies to employment within certain Crown corporations that are agents of the Crown in a province and whose activities are regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This power is explicitly granted through regulation, allowing for flexibility in determining the scope of application.

## Exclusion of Employment from Canada Labour Code Labour Standards

### Section 265 of the Canada Labour Code
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section outlines a specific circumstance under which employment can be excluded from the application of the Canada Labour Code. It applies to employment within corporations acting as agents of the Crown and whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. The Governor in Council has the authority to create regulations specifying these exclusions.

### Section 266 of the Canada Labour Code
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section reinforces the power of the Governor in Council to exclude certain employment from the Canada Labour Code's provisions through regulation. It is very similar to Section 265, indicating a consistent approach to exclusions related to Crown corporations involved in nuclear safety.

### IPG-049_4: Excluded Professions
"Paragraph 167(2)(b) states that “members of such professions as may be designated by regulation” are excluded from the application of Division I."

This interpretation, policy, and guideline highlights that employment within designated professions can be excluded. It states that the Governor in Council can designate professions, and members of those professions are exempt from the application of Division I of the Act. This is achieved through regulation, providing flexibility to define which professions are excluded.

### CLSR-3: Exclusion of Professions
"Section 3 Division I of the Act does not apply to members of the architectural, dental, engineering, legal or medical professions."

This regulation explicitly lists several professions – architectural, dental, engineering, legal, and medical – as being excluded from the application of Division I of the Act. This demonstrates a specific instance of professional exclusion, implemented through the Canada Labour Standards Regulations.

### Labour-Reports-22_10: Provincial and Territorial Variations
"Quebec Legislation - Act respecting  labour standards Definition “Employee” means a person who works for an employer and who is entitled to a wage and also includes a worker who is party to a contract, under which he or she:   undertakes to perform specified work for a person within the scope and in accordance with the methods and means determined by that person undertakes to furnish, for the carrying out of the contract, the material, equipment, raw materials or merchandise chosen by that person and to use them in the manner indicated by him or her..."

This document indicates that provincial and territorial labour standards legislation can have exclusions. Quebec, for example, defines "employee" broadly, but the existence of such legislation allows for the possibility of excluding certain types of workers.

In summary, employment can be excluded from the application of the Canada Labour Code under the following circumstances:

*   **Crown Corporations (Sections 265 & 266):** Employment within corporations acting as agents of the Crown and regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act can be excluded by regulation.
*   **Designated Professions (IPG-049_4 & CLSR-3):**  The Governor in Council can designate specific professions, and members of those professions are excluded from the application of the Act.
*   **Provincial/Territorial Variations (LABOUR-REPORTS-22_10):** Provincial and territorial legislation can have exclusions, although the specific details vary by jurisdiction.

question: How are regulations made under subsection 266(2) of the Canada Labour Code treated in relation to certain procedural requirements typically applied to other sections of the code?
answer:
## Section 266(2) Regulations and Procedural Requirements

### Application of Subsections 121.2(3) to (8)

Section 267 states that
"Subsections 121.2(3) to (8) apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, in respect of a regulation made pursuant to subsection 266(2) except that the references to “subsection (2)” in subsections 121.2(3) to (6) shall be read as references to subsection 266(2)."

This indicates that regulations made under subsection 266(2) are subject to the same procedural requirements as other regulations made under the Canada Labour Code, specifically those outlined in subsections 121.2(3) to (8). The only modification is a substitution of reference; where subsection 121.2(3) to (6) refer to "subsection (2)", they should instead refer to "subsection 266(2)".

### Recommendation of the Minister

Section 266(2) specifies that regulations relating to labour standards in relation to employment subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1) are to be made "On the recommendation of the Minister". This highlights a specific procedural step that must be followed when creating regulations under this subsection.

### Exclusion from Application of the Part

Section 266(1) outlines the purpose of regulations made under subsection (1), which is to
"...exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..." This demonstrates that regulations made under subsection (1) have a significant impact on the application of the Canada Labour Code, potentially excluding certain employment from its scope.

In summary, regulations made under subsection 266(2) are treated similarly to other regulations under the Canada Labour Code in terms of procedural requirements, with the key difference being the requirement for a recommendation from the Minister. They also have a specific application related to excluding certain employment from the scope of the Canada Labour Code, particularly in relation to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

question: What is the scope of application of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART IV - Administrative Monetary Penalties) in relation to departments and their employees?
answer:
## Scope of Application of Part IV of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 268(2) - Limited Application to Part II Violations

Section 268(2) explicitly defines the scope of application for departments and their employees within this Part. It states:
"This Part applies to a department and to persons employed in a department only in respect of a violation that is related to Part II."

This indicates that the administrative monetary penalties outlined in this Part are *not* applicable to violations related to Part III of the Canada Labour Code when they involve departments and their employees. The application is specifically limited to violations connected to Part II.

### Section 268(1) - Definition of "Department"

Section 268(1) provides a definition of "department" for the purpose of this Part:
"...department means a department in, or other portion of, the federal public administration to which Part II applies, as provided under subsection 123(2)."

This definition is crucial because it clarifies which entities are considered "departments" for the purposes of this Part. It is not every entity within the federal public administration, but rather those to which Part II of the Canada Labour Code applies. This means that the application of this Part is tied to the applicability of Part II to a specific department.

In summary, the scope of application of this Part is limited to departments within the federal public administration to which Part II of the Canada Labour Code applies, and only in relation to violations related to Part II.
